culture/abbasid-caliphate.title: Abbasid Caliphate
culture/abbasid-caliphate.summary: The Abbasid Caliphate ruled much of the Islamic world from 750 CE, with its capital at Baghdad, until the Mongols sacked the city in 1258.
facts: Baghdad was founded in 762 and became one of the world's largest cities.
The House of Wisdom and the translation movement drew on Greek, Persian, and Indian works.
Paper manufacturing spread through the caliphate.
Political control fragmented from the 9th century, with regional dynasties taking power.
culture/abbasid-caliphate.context: See Rise of Islam and Al-Khwarizmi. Its end came with Mongol Conquests.
culture/abbasid-caliphate.observer: The Observer notes that a state brought scholars from many traditions into one city, then produced work that neither tradition would have made alone.
questions: How much of the translation effort was state-driven?

culture/aboriginal-australians.title: Aboriginal Australians
culture/aboriginal-australians.summary: Aboriginal Australians are the Indigenous peoples of the Australian mainland, whose ancestors arrived at least 50,000 years ago and whose cultures are among the oldest continuous living traditions.
facts: More than 250 languages were spoken before European colonization in 1788.
Knowledge was passed on through oral traditions, songlines, and ceremony.
Groups managed the landscape with fire and sophisticated ecological knowledge.
Rock art in Australia includes some of the oldest known paintings.
culture/aboriginal-australians.context: See Out of Africa Dispersal and Oceania. Aboriginal societies show that complex culture does not require farming or cities.
culture/aboriginal-australians.observer: The Observer notes that orally preserved knowledge, such as accounts of coastlines flooded at the end of the last ice age, appears to have lasted for millennia. Memory-outsourcing need not use writing to be durable.
questions: How far back do oral traditions preserve accurate events?

culture/achaemenid-persians.title: Achaemenid Persians
culture/achaemenid-persians.summary: The Achaemenid Persians built the largest empire the world had yet seen, founded by Cyrus the Great about 550 BCE and lasting until Alexander's conquest in 330 BCE.
facts: The empire stretched from Egypt and Anatolia to the Indus valley.
It was divided into provinces called satrapies and connected by the Royal Road.
The Cyrus Cylinder is often cited as a record of an imperial policy of tolerance toward local customs.
Zoroastrianism was influential at the Persian court.
culture/achaemenid-persians.context: The empire was ended by Alexander's Conquests. See Iranian Plateau.
culture/achaemenid-persians.observer: The Observer notes an administrative style that governed diverse peoples by preserving their local institutions, an approach that reappears repeatedly in stable empires.
questions: How tolerant was the empire in practice?

culture/al-andalus.title: Al-Andalus
culture/al-andalus.summary: Al-Andalus was the Muslim-ruled part of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492, a region of Muslim, Christian, and Jewish communities that contributed to science, architecture, and literature.
facts: Muslim forces crossed from North Africa into Iberia in 711.
An Umayyad emirate, later a caliphate, ruled from Cordoba from 756.
Cordoba became a large center of learning, and its caliphal library is reputed to have held hundreds of thousands of volumes.
The Alhambra in Granada was built mainly in the 13th and 14th centuries.
Granada, the last Muslim kingdom, fell to Castile and Aragon in January 1492.
culture/al-andalus.context: Al-Andalus grew from the Umayyad Caliphate and was a channel for the knowledge of the Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom into Latin Europe. Its end in 1492 coincided with the start of the Columbian Exchange. Al-Andalus sits in the Medieval Period and the region Mediterranean Basin, and belongs to the theme thread of Religion and Belief and Science and Art and Ritual.
culture/al-andalus.observer: The Observer notes that the same year saw the fall of Granada, the expulsion of Jews from Spain, and the departure of Columbus. A period of pluralism ended as another began that would reshape the planet.
questions: How tolerant was Al-Andalus in practice?

culture/ancestral-puebloans.title: Ancestral Puebloans
culture/ancestral-puebloans.summary: The Ancestral Puebloans built large stone and cliff settlements across the American Southwest from about 700 to 1300 CE, including the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, before drought and hardship led them to disperse into communities that became today's Pueblo peoples.
facts: Their architecture developed from simple pit houses into multi-room stone great houses, most visible today at Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde.
Mesa Verde was occupied from about 450 to 1300 CE, and most of its famous cliff dwellings were built between 1190 and 1300.
Both Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde were abandoned by about 1300 CE.
A prolonged drought from 1276 to 1299, alongside food shortages, is the leading explanation, as communities moved south into what is now Arizona and New Mexico.
Their descendants live today as the Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo peoples of the Rio Grande region.
culture/ancestral-puebloans.context: The Ancestral Puebloans built Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde in North America during the Medieval Period, then dispersed under climatic pressure into the communities that became the Pueblo peoples. See Earth Systems and Life and Art and Ritual.
culture/ancestral-puebloans.observer: The Observer notes that a long drought, rather than conquest or disease, ended two of the era's largest settlement complexes in North America, and that the people who left did not vanish but continued as named communities in the same region. The word "ancestral" acknowledges a continuity that popular labels like "vanished" once denied. A specialist could argue that drought alone cannot explain the timing and manner of abandonment and that social or political strain within the settlements compounded it, which would weaken a purely climatic reading.
questions: How much did social or political conflict contribute to abandonment, alongside drought?
How direct is the line between specific Ancestral Puebloan communities and specific modern Pueblo nations?

culture/ancient-egyptians.title: Ancient Egyptians
culture/ancient-egyptians.summary: The ancient Egyptians built a state along the Nile that lasted, with interruptions, for about three thousand years, until the Roman annexation in 30 BCE.
facts: Their history is divided into kingdoms (Old, Middle, and New) with intermediate periods.
They built pyramids and temples and developed hieroglyphic writing.
Religion emphasized the afterlife, and bodies of the elite were mummified.
The last pharaoh of the Ptolemaic dynasty was Cleopatra VII.
culture/ancient-egyptians.context: See Unification of Egypt, Giza Necropolis, Hatshepsut, and Akhenaten.
culture/ancient-egyptians.observer: The Observer notes an extraordinary investment in the dead: a culture that spent lavishly on stone and craft for the afterlife. See Why the Species Buries Its Dead.
questions: How many people were needed to build the pyramids, and how were they organized?

culture/ancient-greeks.title: Ancient Greeks
culture/ancient-greeks.summary: The ancient Greeks were a group of city-states around the Aegean and beyond, whose politics, philosophy, and art shaped Mediterranean and later world culture.
facts: They developed citizen-based political systems, including Athenian democracy from about 508 BCE.
Philosophers and scientists included Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.
City-states such as Athens and Sparta fought frequently, including the Peloponnesian War (431 to 404 BCE).
The Hellenistic period followed Alexander the Great.
culture/ancient-greeks.context: See Athens and Alexander's Conquests. The Greeks belong to Classical Antiquity.
culture/ancient-greeks.observer: The Observer notes a culture that turned argument into an institution: public debate in assemblies, courts, and schools.
questions: How democratic was Athenian democracy, given exclusions of women, enslaved people, and foreigners?

culture/anglo-saxons.title: Anglo-Saxons
culture/anglo-saxons.summary: The Anglo-Saxons were Germanic-speaking settlers and their descendants who founded the English kingdoms of early medieval Britain, conventionally from the fifth century until the Norman Conquest of 1066. Their language became Old English.
facts: Settlers from North Sea coasts, whom Bede called Angles, Saxons and Jutes, reached eastern and southern Britain from the fifth century (perhaps earlier), as Roman rule ended.
Most Anglo-Saxons farmed in timber-built villages; from the seventh century, trading towns such as Ipswich and Hamwic appeared, and slavery was common.
Small kingdoms, later labelled the seven-kingdom Heptarchy, competed for overlordship; Kent's law code, probably of about 600, set compensation by rank.
Augustine's mission reached Kent in 597; the Sutton Hoo ship burial, early seventh century, held Byzantine silver, and furnished burial largely ended by about 680.
Vikings raided Lindisfarne in 793; Alfred of Wessex beat Guthrum in 878; Cnut conquered England in 1016; Harold Godwinson died at Hastings in 1066.
culture/anglo-saxons.context: The Anglo-Saxons settled Britain, in Europe, during the Medieval Period, as the Romans left and the Fall of the Western Roman Empire unfolded. They shared the island with Celtic-speaking Britons (see Celts), converted to Christianity, and fought the Norse before Norman conquest. See War and Conflict, Kinship and Society and Language and Writing.
culture/anglo-saxons.observer: The Observer notes that the Anglo-Saxons held strangers together through kin-lattice duties priced in wergild, then through a Christian meaning-engine that kings adopted. Their grief-rite moved from goods-filled graves to plain ones, and what survives includes buried gold, monastic manuscripts, and Offa's Dyke, perhaps a claim-line. A specialist could argue that "Anglo-Saxon" was a modern scholars' label more than a felt shared identity, which would weaken a reading of one people held together by shared obligation.
questions: How large was the Anglo-Saxon migration, and how did settlers and Britons interact?
Should "Anglo-Saxon" remain the scholarly label, given debate over its meaning and modern political use?

culture/ayutthaya-kingdom.title: Ayutthaya Kingdom
culture/ayutthaya-kingdom.summary: The Ayutthaya Kingdom was a Tai state in central Thailand that lasted from 1351 to 1767, grew into a major trading power that hosted merchants from Asia and Europe, and ended when Burmese armies destroyed its capital.
facts: The kingdom was founded in 1351 by King Ramathibodi I, also known as U Thong. In foreign accounts it was called Siam, while its own people called themselves Tai and the kingdom Krung Tai.
It became a major regional power and a trading centre where European merchants and Asian traders met. King Narai the Great began diplomatic relations with France during the reign of Louis XIV.

The capital fell to Burmese forces on 7 April 1767 after a siege of fourteen months, and the city was almost completely destroyed. The siege belonged to the Burmese-Siamese War of 1765 to 1767, in which King Hsinbyushin of the Konbaung dynasty sent armies against Ayutthaya.
The kingdom's lifespan is usually given as 417 years. A new capital was established at Thonburi afterwards.
culture/ayutthaya-kingdom.context: Ayutthaya grew in the region formerly dominated by the Khmer Empire, and its long rivalry with Burma continued from the era of the Pagan Kingdom. Its port trade links it to Malacca Sultanate.
culture/ayutthaya-kingdom.observer: The Observer notes a city that knew itself by one name and was recorded abroad by another, which shows how a people's own label and an outsider's may diverge for centuries. The city's destruction, after fourteen months of siege, is recorded as harm to its inhabitants as well as to its monuments.
questions: How many people lived in Ayutthaya at its height, and how many died or were carried off in 1767?
How much of Ayutthaya's wealth came from the trade in the port compared with the surrounding rice lands?

culture/aztec-empire.title: Aztec Empire
culture/aztec-empire.summary: The Aztec (Mexica) Empire was a Triple Alliance of the cities of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan that dominated central Mexico from 1428 until Spanish conquest in 1521.
facts: It collected tribute from conquered city-states.
Tenochtitlan was a large island capital with causeways and floating gardens (chinampas).
Religion included large-scale ritual sacrifice, which Spanish accounts sometimes exaggerated.
Cortes allied with local peoples who resented Aztec tribute, and smallpox devastated the city.
culture/aztec-empire.context: See Tenochtitlan and Mesoamerica. The conquest is part of the Columbian Exchange.
culture/aztec-empire.observer: The Observer notes that the empire fell not to a superior army alone but to alliances, disease, and internal grievances. Systems that rely on tribute create enemies as well as revenue.
questions: How large was the pre-conquest population of central Mexico?

culture/botai-culture.title: Botai Culture
culture/botai-culture.summary: The Botai culture was a society of hunter-herders in northern Kazakhstan, from roughly 3700 to 3100 BCE, who used horses for meat, milk, and probably riding.
facts: Pottery residues show that Botai people used mare's milk by about 3500 BCE, and horse bones show signs of management.
A 2018 study in Science found that Botai horses were not ancestors of modern domestic horses.
Instead, they were ancestors of Przewalski's horses, which are therefore feral descendants of early domesticated horses and not truly wild.
Modern domestic horses derive from a different lineage.
culture/botai-culture.context: The Botai case is central to debates about Animal Domestication and the Indo-European Language Spread. See Central Asian Steppe.
culture/botai-culture.observer: The Observer notes that the first known horse keepers were not the ancestors of the horses that later carried armies. The first domestication seems to have been a dead end.
questions: Where and when did the ancestors of modern domestic horses first come under human control?
fact_checks: 2026-09-26: The Botai culture provides the earliest archaeological evidence for horse husbandry, about 5,500 years ago; Przewalski's horses are the feral descendants of horses herded at Botai, and domestic horses from about 4,000 years ago to the present carry only about 2.7 percent Botai-related ancestry (Science 2018) [Gaunitz et al. 2018 Botai Horses]

2026-09-26: Botai horses (about 3500 BCE) resemble Bronze Age domestic horses, some show signs of bridling, and organic residues in ceramics show processing of mare's milk and carcass products [Outram et al. 2009 Earliest Horse Harnessing and Milking]

culture/buddhism.title: Buddhism
culture/buddhism.summary: Buddhism began in northeastern India between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE with the teaching of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, and spread across Asia into several major traditions, teaching a path out of suffering through insight and practice rather than through a creator god.
facts: Siddhartha Gautama, born a member of a ruling family in the region of present-day Nepal and India, is said to have reached enlightenment and began teaching in his mid-thirties.
His core teaching, the Four Noble Truths, describes suffering, its cause in craving, its end, and a path to that end, aiming at release from the cycle of rebirth, called nirvana.
The faith spread through missionary activity, trade routes and royal patronage, notably under the Mauryan emperor Ashoka.

It developed into three major living traditions: Theravada, dominant in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia; Mahayana, dominant in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam; and Vajrayana, dominant in Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia.
Buddhism has roughly 500 million adherents today, about 6 percent of the world's population.
culture/buddhism.context: Buddhism arose in South Asia during the Iron Age with the teaching of Siddhartha Gautama, part of the broader Axial Age of new philosophical and religious movements, and spread widely under patrons such as Ashoka. See Religion and Belief.
culture/buddhism.observer: The Observer notes that this meaning-engine spread across a continent not primarily by conquest but by teaching, trade and a ruler's patronage, and diversified into traditions different enough in practice that observers sometimes debate whether to treat them as one religion. A specialist could argue that Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana differ enough in text, practice and cosmology that grouping them under one name obscures more than it reveals, which would weaken any single account of "Buddhist belief."
questions: How much unity of belief and practice exists across its major traditions today?
How much of its early spread depended on state patronage such as Ashoka's, versus independent teaching and trade?

culture/byzantine-empire.title: Byzantine Empire
culture/byzantine-empire.summary: The Byzantine Empire is the name given to the eastern Roman Empire, which continued from the founding of Constantinople in 330 CE until the Ottoman conquest in 1453.
facts: Its people called themselves Romans and spoke Greek.
Justinian I (reigned 527 to 565) compiled Roman law and built the Hagia Sophia.
The empire preserved and copied many Greek and Roman texts.
The 1204 sack of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade badly weakened it.
culture/byzantine-empire.context: The empire outlived the Fall of the Western Roman Empire by almost a thousand years. Its capital was Constantinople, and it ended with the Ottoman Empire.
culture/byzantine-empire.observer: The Observer notes that the empire called itself by a name it had inherited long after its Latin-speaking origins faded. Names carry ancestor-weight.
questions: When did the eastern empire become distinctly 'Byzantine'?

culture/casarabe-culture.title: Casarabe Culture
culture/casarabe-culture.summary: The Casarabe culture was a society of the Llanos de Mojos savanna in the Bolivian Amazon, active from about 500 to 1400 CE, whose monumental settlements were revealed by lidar in 2022.
facts: Two large sites, about 147 and 315 hectares, sit at the top of a four-tiered settlement system.
Monumental architecture includes stepped platforms, U-shaped structures, and conical pyramids up to 22 meters tall.
Straight raised causeways, stretching several kilometers, connect the large sites to smaller ones.
The culture area spans roughly 4,500 square kilometers; the settlements show low population density.
culture/casarabe-culture.context: See Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths. The Casarabe sites lay east of the Andes and are among the few known examples of Amazonian low-density urbanism.
culture/casarabe-culture.observer: The Observer notes a society that moved earth on a great scale, building ramps, mounds, and roads, without metal tools or writing that survive. Its planning was legible from the air a thousand years later.
questions: How did Casarabe society organize the labor for its earthworks?

culture/celts.title: Celts
culture/celts.summary: The Celts were related peoples across Iron Age Europe, sharing related languages and, later, the La Tène artistic style, without forming a single state. Rome absorbed most continental Celts, and Celtic language and culture lasted longest in Ireland and parts of Britain.
facts: The Celts were many related tribal groups, including the Gauls of mainland Europe, speaking branches of the Celtic language family such as Gaulish.
The La Tène culture, known for swirling metalwork, flourished from about 450 BCE until Roman conquest, following the earlier Hallstatt culture.
Druids held major religious and political influence in many Celtic societies before Roman conquest, though their role varied by region and period.
Rome attacked the Arverni in 125 BCE, and Julius Caesar completed the conquest of Gaul by 50 BCE despite resistance under leaders such as Vercingetorix.
Rome targeted the druids directly, and continental and southern British Celts were largely assimilated, while Celtic culture lasted longer in Ireland and northern Britain.
culture/celts.context: The Celts inhabited much of Europe during the Iron Age before conquest by the Romans, in a period of wider contact across the ancient world that included Alexander's Conquests. See War and Conflict and Language and Writing.
culture/celts.observer: The Observer notes that "Celtic" names a shared language family and later decorative style across many separate societies, not one people with one story-glue, and that Rome's targeting of the druids suggests it saw their meaning-engine as a source of resistance. Celtic identity lasted where terrain made conquest harder, in Ireland and the far north. A specialist could argue that the umbrella label was applied more consistently by later scholars than by the peoples themselves, which would weaken any reading of the Celts as one self-aware group.
questions: How much shared identity did Celtic-speaking peoples recognize among themselves?
What was the druids' actual political role, and how real was the threat Rome saw in them?

culture/champa.title: Champa
culture/champa.summary: Champa was a group of Cham states along the coast of central and southern Vietnam, dated from 192 CE, that built Hindu temples at My Son, traded across the South China Sea, and was gradually conquered by Vietnam until its last remnant was annexed in 1832.
facts: Champa is usually dated from 192 CE, when the Cham clans of central and southern Vietnam were unified into a single state. The kingdom later broke into separate principalities.

Hinduism, probably brought by Indian merchants, was adopted early and mixed with local traditions and with Buddhist, Khmer, and Chinese influences. By the end of the 10th century Muslim traders had brought Islam.
My Son is a group of Shaiva Hindu temples in central Vietnam, built between the 4th and 13th centuries by Champa's kings.

Vijaya was the capital from 938 until 1471, when the Vietnamese ruler Le Thanh Tong (Lê Thánh Tông) took it and annexed most of the country. One account gives 40,000 Chams killed and 30,000 taken prisoner; these numbers are not independently confirmed.
The remaining principality of Panduranga lasted until 1832, when Emperor Minh Mang began the final conquest and annexed the last of Champa.
culture/champa.context: Champa was a neighbour and rival of the Khmer Empire and its temples at Angkor, and took part in the sea trade of the Indian Ocean Trade Network.
culture/champa.observer: The Observer notes a people who took a meaning-engine from across the sea and made it local, and who were absorbed over centuries by a neighbour to the north. The loss of 1471 is recorded as harm: a capital taken, people killed or carried off, and a state reduced to a remnant that lasted another three and a half centuries.
questions: How reliable are the reported casualty figures for the fall of Vijaya?
How did Cham communities that survive today (Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist) keep their identity after annexation?

culture/cherokee.title: Cherokee
culture/cherokee.summary: The Cherokee are a people native to the southeastern United States whose nation adopted a written syllabary in the 1820s and survived the forced removal known as the Trail of Tears, continuing today as several federally recognized nations including the Eastern Band in North Carolina.
facts: At European contact in the sixteenth century the Cherokee held a homeland spanning parts of present-day North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Alabama and Tennessee.
Sequoyah completed an 85-character syllabary for Cherokee in 1821, after twelve years of work, enabling mass literacy within a short time.
In 1838 and 1839 United States troops under General Winfield Scott forcibly removed most Cherokee to territory west of the Mississippi, a journey remembered as the Trail of Tears, in which many died.
Some Cherokee avoided removal by hiding in the North Carolina mountains or claiming state citizenship. Their descendants formed the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, based on the Qualla Boundary.
The Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma and the Eastern Band are among the largest Native American nations in the United States today.
culture/cherokee.context: The Cherokee homeland lay in North America. Sequoyah's syllabary gave the nation a written mark-code shortly before the Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears in the Industrial Age. See Language and Writing and Kinship and Society.
culture/cherokee.observer: The Observer notes that a nation given a new mark-code for its own language in the 1820s kept records and petitions with it through the removal that tried to end its presence in its homeland. The split into an Eastern Band and a western nation shows one people's story continuing along two claim-lines after a single act of state violence. A specialist could argue that literacy's role in Cherokee survival is overstated relative to land, kinship networks and legal strategy, which would weaken a reading that credits the syllabary alone.
questions: How much did literacy, as opposed to other factors, shape Cherokee resistance to removal?
How do the histories of the Eastern Band and the Oklahoma nation compare since their separation?

culture/chinchorro-culture.title: Chinchorro Culture
culture/chinchorro-culture.summary: The Chinchorro were fisher-hunter-gatherers of the Atacama Desert coast in what is now northern Chile and southern Peru, known for the earliest deliberate artificial mummification, which began by about 5050 BCE.
facts: The Chinchorro lived on the coast from about 5450 to 890 BCE.
They preserved men, women, and children of the community, not only an elite, by reconstructing bodies with clay, wigs, and mineral pigments.
The tradition lasted about 3,000 years, ending about 1800 BCE.
UNESCO inscribed the settlement and mummification sites as a World Heritage Site in 2021.
culture/chinchorro-culture.context: The Chinchorro's practice is the earliest known artificial mummification, thousands of years before the Ancient Egyptians. See Why the Species Buries Its Dead and Andes.
culture/chinchorro-culture.observer: The Observer notes that a culture of coastal foragers invested in preserving the dead, including children, before farming or cities. The grief-rite is older than the state.
questions: Why did the Chinchorro begin to preserve their dead?

culture/chola-dynasty.title: Chola Dynasty
culture/chola-dynasty.summary: The Chola dynasty ruled much of southern India from around 850 to 1279 CE and was a naval power that traded and fought across the Bay of Bengal.
facts: Vijayalaya Chola captured Thanjavur around 850 CE.
Rajaraja I (r. 985 to 1014) built the Brihadisvara Temple in Thanjavur, completed around 1010, now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Rajendra I sent a naval expedition against Srivijaya around 1025.
The Cholas traded with China and Southeast Asia.
Chola bronzes, including the dancing Shiva (Nataraja), are celebrated works of art.
culture/chola-dynasty.context: The Cholas were one of the strongest states in the Indian Ocean Trade Network, competing with Srivijaya for control of the sea lanes. Chola Dynasty sits in the Medieval Period and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Trade and Economy and War and Conflict and Art and Ritual.
culture/chola-dynasty.observer: The Observer notes that an inland-looking temple-building state used its fleet to project power across an ocean. Its long-distance raid was unusual for its time and shows that maritime strength was not limited to coastal traders.
questions: What was the purpose of the Chola expedition to Srivijaya?

culture/christianity.title: Christianity
culture/christianity.summary: Christianity began among followers of Jesus of Nazareth in first-century Roman Judea and spread through the Mediterranean world to become the most widely practiced religion in the world.
facts: Jesus of Nazareth was executed by Roman authority in Jerusalem, most likely between 29 and 33 CE. His followers believed he had risen from death, and this belief became the basis of the new movement.
Paul of Tarsus, a former persecutor of the movement, became its most active early missionary, founding communities among non-Jews across the Roman Empire and shaping much of its early theology.
Within about a century, Christian communities existed across Greece, Syria, Armenia, North Africa and beyond.
The faith split into Eastern Orthodoxy and the Catholic Church in the Great Schism of 1054, and the Reformation of 1517 produced Protestant churches, giving three main branches today.
Christianity has about 2.4 billion adherents, roughly a third of the world's population, the Catholic Church alone counting about 1.3 billion members.
culture/christianity.context: Christianity arose in the Levant and Anatolia within the Roman Empire during Classical Antiquity, later becoming the state religion of the Byzantine Empire and, centuries afterward, existing alongside the Rise of Islam in the same region. See Religion and Belief.
culture/christianity.observer: The Observer notes that a movement built around the death of one man became, through a convert who had once opposed it, a story-glue that crossed the ordinary claim-lines of ethnicity within the Roman world within a single century. Two later splits, in 1054 and 1517, show the same meaning-engine repeatedly dividing over authority and practice while its central claims persisted. A specialist could argue that its early rapid growth owed as much to Roman roads and common language as to the message itself, which would weaken a reading that credits the spread to doctrine alone.
questions: How much of Christianity's early spread reflects the message versus the infrastructure of the Roman Empire it grew within?
How do its many branches today compare in how they trace authority back to the earliest community?

culture/confucianism.title: Confucianism
culture/confucianism.summary: Confucianism is a Chinese tradition of ethics and social order built on the teaching of Confucius (551 to 479 BCE), which became the official ideology of imperial China under the Han dynasty and shaped government and family life across East Asia.
facts: Confucius was an itinerant teacher during China's Warring States period who sought but largely failed to gain lasting influence as a government adviser in his own lifetime.
His disciples compiled his sayings after his death as the Analects, the central text of the tradition.
A key teaching, filial piety, extends genuine respect and care for parents into a model for loyalty within the wider political order.

Under the Han dynasty, Confucianism became the state's official ideology, and an imperial examination system tested officials on Confucian texts, a practice that shaped Chinese government for centuries.
The tradition spread beyond China to Vietnam, Korea and Japan, shaping their systems of government and social norms, including their own examination systems modeled on China's.
culture/confucianism.context: Confucianism developed in East Asia during the Iron Age through the teaching of Confucius, part of the wider Axial Age, and became state orthodoxy under the Han Dynasty. See Religion and Belief and Kinship and Society.
culture/confucianism.observer: The Observer notes that a teacher who failed to secure influence in his own time became, centuries after his death, the ancestor-weight behind an empire's entire method of selecting officials, with filial duty inside the kin-lattice serving as the template for loyalty to the state itself. A specialist could argue that the Han state's adoption of Confucianism reflects the state's own need for a stabilizing ideology as much as the teaching's inherent merit, which would weaken a reading of its rise as owed to its ideas alone.
questions: How much did the Han state's adoption of Confucianism serve the state's own interests, apart from the teaching's content?
How uniformly was Confucianism practiced across China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam?

culture/daoism.title: Daoism
culture/daoism.summary: Daoism is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in harmony with the Dao, "the Way," traditionally traced to the sage Laozi and later developed into organized religious movements alongside its philosophical school.
facts: Laozi, traditionally placed in the sixth century BCE, is credited as the founding figure, though modern scholars think the text attributed to him, the Dao De Jing, was likely compiled by multiple hands after his time.
Zhuangzi (about 369 to 286 BCE) was a major later interpreter, and the book bearing his name is considered even more wide-ranging than the Dao De Jing.
Its central principle, wuwei, "nonaction," describes spontaneity and noninterference with the natural order rather than passive idleness.
Organized religious Daoism began later, marked by the Celestial Masters movement founded when Zhang Daoling reported revelations from a deified Laozi in 142 CE.
Daoist philosophy and religious practice both continued alongside Confucianism in Chinese life, sometimes overlapping with folk religion, making a precise adherent count difficult to give.
culture/daoism.context: Daoism developed in East Asia during the Iron Age through the teaching attributed to Laozi, continuing as a distinct tradition alongside Confucianism into the Han Dynasty and after. See Religion and Belief.
culture/daoism.observer: The Observer notes that a philosophy built around noninterference and yielding became, centuries after its founding figure's traditional dates, the ancestor-weight behind an organized religious movement claiming revelation from that same figure now treated as a deity, a shift from teaching to meaning-engine. A specialist could argue that "Daoism" groups together a philosophical school and a family of religious movements with looser connections than the shared name implies, which would weaken any single account of Daoist belief.
questions: How much continuity exists between the philosophical Daoism of Laozi and Zhuangzi and the later religious movements that claimed their authority?
How separable is Daoist practice from Chinese folk religion in everyday life?

culture/delhi-sultanate.title: Delhi Sultanate
culture/delhi-sultanate.summary: The Delhi Sultanate was a series of five Muslim dynasties that ruled much of northern India from 1206 until Babur's victory at Panipat in 1526.
facts: It began after the conquests of Muhammad of Ghor, and Qutb al-Din Aibak became the first sultan.
The five dynasties were the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, and Lodi.
It resisted several Mongol invasions in the 13th century.
Timur sacked Delhi in 1398.
It was replaced by the Mughal Empire after the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
culture/delhi-sultanate.context: The sultanate connected northern India to the wider Islamic world, faced the Mongol Empire, suffered the raid of Timur, and was followed by the Mughal Empire. Delhi Sultanate sits in the Medieval Period and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
culture/delhi-sultanate.observer: The Observer notes that in this era a state could be led by former slave soldiers and still survive Mongol invasions and repeated dynastic changes. Legitimacy appears to rest more on military competence and patronage than on ancestry.
questions: How did Delhi's rulers manage a largely non-Muslim population?

culture/etruscans.title: Etruscans
culture/etruscans.summary: The Etruscans were a people of Etruria in central Italy, roughly modern Tuscany and northern Lazio, whose city-states flourished from about the eighth to the third century BCE. Rome gradually conquered and absorbed them.
facts: Etruscan city-states included Tarquinia, Cerveteri, Vulci and Veii. Livy describes a league of twelve peoples meeting at Voltumna's shrine.
Their wealth came from farming, metals and sea trade. Populonia smelted Elba iron ore, and ports such as Pyrgi linked Etruria with Greeks and Phoenicians.
They wrote a non-Indo-European language in a Greek-derived alphabet. Gold tablets from Pyrgi, with Etruscan and Phoenician texts, date to about 500 BCE.
Etruscans and Carthaginians fought Phocaean Greeks at Alalia about 540 BCE, and Greek fleets defeated the Etruscans at Cumae in 474 BCE.
Rome traditionally took Veii in 396 BCE and sacked Volsinii in 264 BCE. Etruscans gained Roman citizenship around 90 BCE, and their language survived into the first century CE.
culture/etruscans.context: The Etruscans flourished in Europe from the Iron Age, trading with the Ancient Greeks, Phoenicians and Carthage before absorption by the Romans. Etruscan writing was a probable route for the Alphabet into Latin. See Trade and Economy, Religion and Belief and Art and Ritual.
culture/etruscans.observer: The Observer notes that Etruscan cities shared a meaning-engine and sound-code rather than one state, and Roman writers describe ritual books that treated a claim-line as a sacred act. At Cerveteri, their grief-rite laid out a cemetery as streets of houses for the dead, and with Etruscan books largely lost, tombs and short inscriptions remain. A specialist could argue that the league's unity was partly a Greek and Roman simplification, which would weaken reading the Etruscans as one community.
questions: Did the Etruscans see themselves as one people, or as citizens of separate cities?
How far did Etruscan rulers shape early Rome, given that stories of Etruscan kings are partly legendary?

culture/franks.title: Franks
culture/franks.summary: The Franks were a Germanic people who moved into Roman Gaul and built one of early medieval Europe's most powerful kingdoms, first under the Merovingian dynasty of Clovis I and later under the Carolingians, whose most famous ruler was Charlemagne.
facts: The Franks appear in Roman records in the third century CE on the lower Rhine and expanded into Gaul as Roman power weakened.
Clovis I of the Merovingian dynasty defeated the last major Roman official in Gaul in 486 and had united the Frankish tribes by about 501.
Clovis converted to Catholic Christianity, and his people's adoption of it helped unite the Franks and set them apart from neighboring Germanic kingdoms that followed other Christian traditions.
The Merovingians ruled until the eighth century, when Pepin the Short, with papal support, founded the Carolingian dynasty.

The Carolingian kingdom peaked under Charlemagne and later divided among his descendants. Its territories became the basis of medieval France, Germany and the Holy Roman Empire (not yet a vault note).
culture/franks.context: The Franks built their kingdom in Europe during the early Medieval Period, filling the space left by the Fall of the Western Roman Empire. Their empire under Charlemagne was an ancestor of the Holy Roman Empire (not yet a vault note). See War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
culture/franks.observer: The Observer notes that a ruler's personal conversion to his Roman subjects' majority faith became story-glue that welded conquerors and conquered into one people, setting the Franks apart from rival kingdoms that kept a minority creed. Two centuries later a change of dynasty was legitimized by the same meaning-engine, papal blessing replacing a discredited bloodline. A specialist could argue that Clovis's conversion served political advantage with his Gallo-Roman subjects as much as belief, which would weaken a reading of it as faith alone.
questions: How much of Clovis's conversion reflects conviction versus calculated alliance with his Gallo-Roman subjects?
How unified was Frankish identity across the peoples the Merovingians and Carolingians ruled?

culture/funan.title: Funan
culture/funan.summary: Funan is the Chinese name for a polity, perhaps a league of towns, in the Mekong delta and Cambodia from about the 1st to the 6th century CE. It is known from Chinese records and Oc Eo excavations; no known local text uses the name.
facts: A canal of 70-80 km linked the port of Oc Eo to Angkor Borei, likely for transport and water management.
Oc Eo yielded Roman gold medallions of Antoninus Pius, and possibly Marcus Aurelius, plus Indian and Persian objects.
Chinese sources credit the early 3rd-century king Fan Shiman with a fleet and attacks on more than ten kingdoms. Later histories quote envoys Kang Tai and Zhu Ying on walled towns and archives.
Funan practiced Hinduism and Buddhism, with Sanskrit inscriptions.
Chinese records list envoys from Funan's last known king, Rudravarman, until 539. Chenla is said to have annexed Funan between the 6th century and about 627; scholars dispute how.
culture/funan.context: Funan lay in Southeast Asia during Classical Antiquity, beside Champa and on Indian Ocean Trade Network sea routes that brought Hinduism and Buddhism. Its canals in the Mekong River delta relate to other Irrigation Canals, and the later Khmer Empire arose nearby. See Trade and Economy and Religion and Belief.
culture/funan.observer: The Observer notes Funan drew Roman, Indian and Persian goods into one exchange-web, while its rulers' Indian religion and script may have worked as a status-signal binding strangers. Canals and statues remain, but Funan's name and claim-lines come mostly from outsiders' texts. A specialist could argue that Funan was a loose set of allied ports, not one state, which would weaken reading it as one realm with one story-glue.
questions: Was Funan one kingdom, or several centers Chinese writers treated as one?
Did Chenla conquer Funan, or did power shift among Cambodian centers?
What did Funan's people call themselves, and what language did they speak?

culture/garifuna.title: Garifuna
culture/garifuna.summary: The Garifuna are an Afro-Indigenous people who formed on St Vincent from African and Kalinago ancestry, were deported by Britain to Central America in 1797, and now live along the Caribbean coast from Belize to Nicaragua.
facts: Tradition traces Garifuna origins to Africans from Spanish slave ships wrecked near St Vincent (1635 or about 1675); no eyewitness account is known, and many historians instead favor runaways from nearby islands.
Garifuna women grew cassava and made ereba bread while men fished; remittances now supplement many rural incomes.
Chatoyer, a Black Carib leader, resisted British expansion in the First Carib War (1769-1773), and was killed on 14 March 1795 in the Second Carib War.
Britain deported over 4,000 Garifuna to Baliceaux from 1796, where about half died; about 2,000 landed on Roatan on 12 April 1797, and most then moved to Trujillo.
UNESCO proclaimed Garifuna language, dance and music in 2001; in 2015 the Inter-American Court found Honduras violated two Garifuna communities' collective property rights.
culture/garifuna.context: The Garifuna took shape in the Caribbean and Atlantic World during the Early Modern Period, through the Atlantic Slave Trade and alongside the Kalinago. Their 1790s war and deportation fell within the Age of Revolutions. See War and Conflict, Kinship and Society and Language and Writing.
culture/garifuna.observer: The Observer notes that the Garifuna joined African and Kalinago ancestry into a kin-lattice, sustained by a sound-code and the dugu ancestor rite through an exile that killed thousands. The 1773 treaty's claim-line did not hold, and Honduran titling later failed some Garifuna communities, the Inter-American Court found. A specialist could argue that the shipwreck story is a later founding narrative, which would weaken any reading dating the kin-lattice to one seventeenth-century event.
questions: How much of the shipwreck story rests on documented events rather than later tradition?
How did Arawakan grammar and Carib-derived vocabulary come to combine in Garifuna speech?

culture/ghana-empire.title: Ghana Empire
culture/ghana-empire.summary: The Ghana Empire, called Wagadu by its own people, was a Soninke state in the western Sahel whose wealth rested on the trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt, and ivory. Its exact extent, its end, and the role of outside conquest are debated.
facts: The empire lay in what is now southeastern Mauritania, western Mali, and eastern Senegal. Most scholars accept an origin in the 8th or 9th century.

The Soninke people formed its foundation. Its wealth was linked to the growth of regular trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt, and ivory, which supported larger towns and territorial expansion to control trade routes.

The capital is believed to have been at Koumbi Saleh, on the edge of the Sahara. The description left by al-Bakri in 1067 or 1068 says the capital consisted of two towns joined by continuous habitations.
Some accounts say the capital was sacked about 1076 by the Almoravids of North Africa, perhaps in retaliation for Ghana's attempt to control trade held by Saharan commercial centres.

The empire declined in the 12th century, when competing trade routes opened further east and a prolonged dry spell hurt agriculture. Tradition says the city was destroyed by Sundiata in 1240 and what remained was absorbed into the Mali Empire.
culture/ghana-empire.context: Ghana was the first of the large Sahelian states that the Mali Empire and later the Songhai Empire followed. Its story is tied to the spread of Islam through the Sahara; see Rise of Islam.
culture/ghana-empire.observer: The Observer notes an exchange-web whose wealth was carried on paths and rainfall, and which, on these accounts, came apart through shifting routes and drought more than through a single blow. A network that looks like a state is only as fixed as the roads and climate under it.
questions: Did the Almoravids actually conquer Ghana, or is that a later simplification of a slower decline?
How much of what is known about the capital comes from outside observers, and how much from excavation?

culture/gupta-empire.title: Gupta Empire
culture/gupta-empire.summary: The Gupta Empire ruled much of northern India from about 320 to 550 CE and is often associated with a flowering of mathematics, astronomy, and the arts.
facts: The astronomer and mathematician Aryabhata (born 476) worked in this period and gave an accurate value of pi.
The decimal place-value system with zero as a digit was developed in India; see Zero and Place-Value Notation.
Nalanda, a major Buddhist center of learning, flourished.
'Golden Age' is a later label; historians debate how far it applies.
culture/gupta-empire.context: The Gupta period belongs to South Asia in Classical Antiquity. Its mathematics passed westward through scholars such as Al-Khwarizmi.
culture/gupta-empire.observer: The Observer notes that mathematical ideas developed in one place travelled far. A symbol for 'nothing' changed how numbers work across Eurasia.
questions: How much of 'Gupta science' was specific to the empire versus the wider Indian tradition?

culture/gokturk-khaganate.title: Göktürk Khaganate
culture/gokturk-khaganate.summary: The Göktürk Khaganate was a Turkic steppe empire, founded about 552 CE by Bumin Khagan, that stretched across Inner Asia and left the earliest known Turkic writing.
facts: The First Turkic Khaganate lasted from 552 to 603; a Second Khaganate followed from about 682 to 744.
The Orkhon inscriptions, erected between 732 and 735 in Mongolia to honor Kul Tigin and his brother Bilge Khagan, are the oldest known Turkic writing.
They use a runic-like Old Turkic script and were discovered in 1889.
Sogdian was a court language for writing documents.
culture/gokturk-khaganate.context: The Göktürks followed the Xiongnu tradition of steppe empire and dealt with the Tang Dynasty and the Sogdians. Later Turkic peoples spread across Asia and Anatolia.
culture/gokturk-khaganate.observer: The Observer notes a people who carved their history in stone to speak to the future, and in their own language, after long being described by others. The inscriptions are a self-portrait of a steppe empire.
questions: How did the two Khaganates relate to each other?

culture/han-dynasty.title: Han Dynasty
culture/han-dynasty.summary: The Han dynasty ruled China from 206 BCE to 220 CE and consolidated the imperial system begun under Qin, so that 'Han' is still the name of the majority ethnic group.
facts: It expanded westward and opened contact with Central Asia; see Opening of the Silk Roads.
A census in 2 CE recorded about 58 million people.
Confucian learning became the basis of state education.
Paper and other inventions were developed under the Han.
culture/han-dynasty.context: The Han built on Unification of China under Qin and on the ideas of Confucius. See Paper.
culture/han-dynasty.observer: The Observer notes that the dynasty gave a name and a canon to a whole cultural sphere. A state that lasts four centuries turns its administrative habits into identity.
questions: How large was the Han state relative to Rome?

culture/haudenosaunee-confederacy.title: Haudenosaunee Confederacy
culture/haudenosaunee-confederacy.summary: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy is a political union of Indigenous nations in the northeastern woodlands of North America, formed centuries before European contact.
facts: The original five nations were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca; the Tuscarora joined in the 18th century.
The Great Law of Peace is the oral constitution of the confederacy.
Clan mothers have the power to appoint and remove chiefs.
Estimates of the founding date range from about 1142 to the 15th century; scholars disagree.
culture/haudenosaunee-confederacy.context: The confederacy is an example of a durable non-state political union in North America. Its influence on the U.S. founding is debated.
culture/haudenosaunee-confederacy.observer: The Observer notes a federation formed from warring peoples through a shared founding story. Story-glue can bind peoples as well as kings can.
questions: When was the confederacy formed?
How much did it influence colonial political thinking?

culture/hawaiian-kingdom.title: Hawaiian Kingdom
culture/hawaiian-kingdom.summary: The Hawaiian Kingdom was a Native Hawaiian monarchy united by Kamehameha I between about 1795 and 1810 and overthrown in 1893. The United States annexed the islands in 1898; the annexation's legality remains disputed.
facts: Kamehameha I conquered Oʻahu in 1795 and gained Kauaʻi and Niʻihau by negotiation in 1810; sources differ on the founding year.
The Hawaiian Kingdom's farmers worked taro terraces and fishponds in mountain-to-sea ahupuaʻa; exports shifted from sandalwood to sugar, boosted by an 1875 United States treaty.
The kapu system of taboos ended in 1819, a written constitution followed in 1840, and Britain and France recognized independence in 1843.

Introduced diseases cut the Native Hawaiian population to about 71,000 by 1853. After the 1848 Great Māhele, commoners' successful claims under the 1850 Kuleana Act covered under one percent of the land.

An armed militia forced the 1887 Bayonet Constitution on Kalākaua. In 1893 a Committee of Safety, with United States Marines ashore, deposed Liliuokalani. About 21,000 petitioned against annexation in 1897; Congress annexed the islands in 1898.
culture/hawaiian-kingdom.context: The Hawaiian Kingdom, from Kamehameha I to Liliuokalani, ruled descendants of the Polynesians (Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific) and, later, many immigrants in Oceania during the Industrial Age. See War and Conflict, Trade and Economy and Kinship and Society.
culture/hawaiian-kingdom.observer: The Observer notes that the Hawaiian Kingdom merged rival chiefdoms into one kin-lattice, then entered treaties and constitutions in its recognizers' mark-code. The same tools, including the Māhele's tradable claim-lines, let American- and European-descended businessmen gather power against the monarchy. A specialist could argue that coercion in 1887 and 1893, not the tools, caused the loss, which would weaken a reading that finds the loss built into them.
questions: How large was the Hawaiian population in 1778, given estimates from 110,000 to over 800,000?
Did the Hawaiian Kingdom survive as a state in international law after 1893, as some scholars argue?

culture/hinduism.title: Hinduism
culture/hinduism.summary: Hinduism is a family of religious traditions native to South Asia that grew out of the ancient Vedic religion, has no single founder or founding event, and today counts about 1.2 billion adherents, most of them in India.
facts: Its earliest texts, the Vedas, were composed roughly in the mid-second millennium BCE, and its philosophical Upanishads later explored ideas of the soul and the cycle of rebirth.
Rather than one founder, it developed over centuries by fusing regional and cultural traditions, so no single origin date or figure can be given.
A central concept, brahman, describes an ultimate reality identified with the individual soul, or atman.
Its two largest branches are Vaishnavism, centered on devotion to Vishnu, and Shaivism, centered on Shiva, each containing many further traditions.
About 1.2 billion people practice Hinduism today, roughly 15 percent of the world's population, with about 1.1 billion living in India.
culture/hinduism.context: Hinduism's roots reach into the Indus Valley Civilization and the Vedic Period in South Asia during the Bronze Age, and the tradition was later patronized and contested under states such as the Maurya Empire. See Religion and Belief.
culture/hinduism.observer: The Observer notes that a tradition without a single founder or a single scripture managing to organize a sixth of humanity's population under one broad name suggests story-glue that operates by accretion rather than by a single unifying claim, closer to a family of related meaning-engines than one system. A specialist could argue that grouping such varied regional practices under one word "Hinduism," itself coined by outsiders, imposes a unity the traditions did not claim for themselves, which would weaken any single account of "what Hindus believe."
questions: How far can practices as different as regional Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions be treated as one religion?
How much of the modern term "Hinduism" reflects a category imposed from outside rather than one adherents used for themselves?

culture/hittites.title: Hittites
culture/hittites.summary: The Hittites were a Bronze Age people of Anatolia who built an empire from their capital Hattusa, speaking the earliest attested Indo-European language.
facts: Hattusa lies near modern Bogazkale in central Turkey, and its archive of cuneiform tablets was found in the early 20th century.
Hittite is the oldest recorded Indo-European language; Bedrich Hrozny showed its Indo-European nature in 1915.
Hittite forces raided Babylon around 1595 BCE, according to the conventional chronology.
The Hittites fought Egypt at the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BCE, and later made a treaty with Ramesses II, around 1259 BCE.
The empire collapsed around 1200 to 1180 BCE in the Bronze Age Collapse.
culture/hittites.context: The Hittites are a key witness to the early spread of Indo-European languages, see Indo-European Language Spread. They contested power with the Ancient Egyptians at the Battle of Kadesh and fell in the Bronze Age Collapse. culture/inca-empire.title: Inca Empire
culture/inca-empire.summary: The Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu) was the largest state of the pre-Columbian Americas, ruling millions of people along the Andes from about 1438 until Spanish conquest in 1533.
facts: Its capital was Cusco, and its road system extended roughly 30,000 to 40,000 kilometers.
It recorded information on knotted cords called quipu.
The state exacted labor service (mit'a) rather than money taxes.
Civil war and smallpox weakened it before Pizarro's arrival.

culture/indus-valley-civilization.title: Indus Valley Civilization
culture/indus-valley-civilization.summary: The Indus Valley Civilization (also called the Harappan) was a Bronze Age urban culture of the Indus River basin, at its height around 2600 to 1900 BCE.
facts: Major cities included Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.
Cities had planned streets and drainage, and goods were made to standard weights.
It traded with Mesopotamia.
Its script has not been deciphered.

culture/indus-valley-civilization.observer: The Observer notes the puzzle of a large urban society with few obvious palaces or royal monuments, which challenges the assumption that cities always come with kings.

culture/inuit-and-the-thule-expansion.title: Inuit and the Thule Expansion
culture/inuit-and-the-thule-expansion.summary: The Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, spread from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland beginning around 1000 CE, replacing the earlier Dorset culture.
facts: The Thule culture emerged in the Bering Strait region around 900 to 1000 CE.
Its people used dog sleds, skin boats (umiaks and kayaks), and toggling harpoons for hunting whales and seals.
They expanded east across Arctic Canada and reached Greenland by roughly the 12th to 13th century.
Genetic studies show the earlier Dorset population was largely replaced rather than assimilated.
Norse colonists lived in southern Greenland from about 985 CE until the 15th century.
culture/inuit-and-the-thule-expansion.context: The Thule expansion carried people originating from Beringia's region across the Arctic and brought them into contact with the Norse. Its scale is comparable to the pastoral traditions of the Yakut (Sakha) in Siberia. Inuit and the Thule Expansion sits in the Medieval Period and the region Siberia and the Arctic, and belongs to the theme thread of Technology and Kinship and Society.
culture/inuit-and-the-thule-expansion.observer: The Observer notes that a hunting technology suited to ice, with boats, sleds, and harpoons, allowed a small population to occupy a huge cold region in just a few centuries. Technology, not numbers, set the pace of the expansion.
questions: What led to the Dorset population's decline?

culture/islam.title: Islam
culture/islam.summary: Islam is the religion founded by Muhammad in seventh-century Arabia, centered on the Quran as the word of God and on the practices set out in its five pillars, and today the second-largest religion in the world.
facts: Muslims hold that Muhammad, an Arabian merchant, began receiving revelations from God around 610 CE, later compiled as the Quran, and that he united the tribes of Arabia under the new faith before his death in 632.

A dispute over his successor split his followers soon after his death: most accepted the elected caliphs (becoming Sunni), while a smaller group held that leadership belonged to his family through his son-in-law Ali (becoming Shia).
The faith spread rapidly under the early caliphates, then under empires such as the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates, from Spain to Central and South Asia within a few centuries.
Sunni Muslims make up roughly 85 percent of the world's estimated 1.9 billion Muslims, and Shia Muslims about 15 percent, with Shia forming the majority in Iran, Iraq, Bahrain and Azerbaijan.
culture/islam.context: Islam began in the Arabian Peninsula with Muhammad at the start of the Medieval Period, part of the Rise of Islam, and spread through empires including the Umayyad Caliphate and Abbasid Caliphate. See Religion and Belief.
culture/islam.observer: The Observer notes that a succession dispute settled within a generation of the founder's death created a claim-line, Sunni against Shia, that fourteen centuries of later history have not erased, showing how a single kin-lattice question about legitimate leadership can outlast the empires built around it. A specialist could argue that many local and political factors, not the original dispute alone, kept the split alive in specific regions, which would weaken a reading of the divide as a single continuous grievance.
questions: How much of the continuing Sunni-Shia distinction reflects the original succession dispute versus later political history?
What let the faith spread so quickly across such different regions within its first century?

culture/jainism.title: Jainism
culture/jainism.summary: Jainism is an ancient Indian religion centered on non-violence toward all living things, taught by a line of teachers called tirthankaras and traditionally traced to Mahavira in the sixth century BCE, though the tradition itself holds its teaching to be eternal.
facts: Mahavira, traditionally dated about 599 to 527 BCE, is remembered as the twenty-fourth and final tirthankara of the current cosmic cycle, and is sometimes called the founder of Jainism as practiced today. Jain tradition itself considers its teaching timeless rather than founded by any one person.
Mahavira reportedly renounced a noble upbringing at about 30 and practiced severe asceticism for over a decade before reaching what Jains call perfect knowledge.

Its central principle, ahimsa, non-violence toward all living beings, is practiced to an unusual degree by Jain monks and nuns, some of whom sweep their path and cover their mouths to avoid harming small creatures.
The tradition split into two main branches, Digambara and Svetambara, by about the fourth century CE, differing over practices such as monastic clothing.
Roughly four to five million Jains live today, the great majority in India, with smaller communities in East Africa, North America and Europe.
culture/jainism.context: Jainism developed in South Asia during the Iron Age, in the same broad period as Siddhartha Gautama's teaching and the wider Axial Age of new religious movements. See Religion and Belief.
culture/jainism.observer: The Observer notes that a small community has sustained one of the most demanding versions of nonviolence recorded among the world's meaning-engines for over two thousand years, treating harm to the smallest creature as morally weighty. A specialist could argue that Mahavira's dates and the very idea of Jainism as a distinct tradition beginning with him are themselves later constructions over a longer, less clearly bounded history of ascetic teaching, which would weaken any precise founding date.
questions: How much of the traditional account of Mahavira's life reflects history versus later hagiography?
How consistent has the practice of ahimsa been across Jain communities and periods?

culture/jomon-culture.title: Jomon Culture
culture/jomon-culture.summary: The Jomon were hunter-gatherer-fishers of the Japanese archipelago who made some of the world's earliest pottery and lived in settled villages for about 14,000 years before rice farming arrived.
facts: The name Jomon means cord-marked, after the patterns pressed into their pottery.
Some of the earliest Jomon pottery is dated to around 16,000 years ago.
They made clay figurines called dogu.
The site of Sannai-Maruyama in Aomori was occupied for about 1,700 years, from around 3900 BCE.
Rice-farming migrants, the Yayoi, arrived from the continent beginning around the first millennium BCE, and the dates are debated.
culture/jomon-culture.context: The Jomon show that Pottery and sedentary life preceded The Agricultural Revolution in this region. Rice farming, as described in Domestication of Rice, entered later. Jomon Culture sits in the Neolithic and the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Art and Ritual and Technology.
culture/jomon-culture.observer: The Observer notes that the Jomon lived in permanent villages and made elaborate pots without farming, which shows that the sequence of fire, farming, and settlement is not universal. Settling does not require agriculture.
questions: How did the Jomon and Yayoi populations interact?

culture/judaism.title: Judaism
culture/judaism.summary: Judaism is the religion and communal tradition of the Jewish people, tracing its origins to the patriarch Abraham and the covenant given to Moses at Sinai, and organized for most of its history around a body of law and commentary rather than a central authority.
facts: Tradition dates Abraham, regarded as the first Hebrew and forefather of the Jewish people, to about 2000 to 1800 BCE, though this is traditional rather than documented history.
Its founding text is the Torah, the five books attributed to Moses, later joined by other scriptures collected as the Hebrew Bible.
The Second Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed by Rome in 70 CE. Without a central temple, rabbis took over interpreting the Torah, producing extensive commentary later compiled as the Talmud.
Today's main movements, Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist, range from traditional to progressive in how they apply Jewish law.
Worldwide adherents numbered about 15 million as of the early 2020s, most living in Israel and the United States.
culture/judaism.context: Judaism's traditional origins lie in the Levant and Anatolia in the Bronze Age, among the empires of ancient Mesopotamia such as the Sumerians, and its history includes conquest by the Neo-Assyrian Empire and later the Rise of Islam in the same region. See Religion and Belief.
culture/judaism.observer: The Observer notes that the destruction of a single building in 70 CE redirected an entire tradition's meaning-engine from temple sacrifice toward text and interpretation, a shift in memory-outsourcing that let the community persist without a capital. Adherents hold the tradition's core claims as historical and covenantal; a specialist could argue that its earliest patriarchal accounts describe an ancestor-weight built up over centuries of retelling rather than a documented individual, which would weaken any confident dating of its earliest layer.
questions: How much of the patriarchal narrative reflects documented history versus later tradition?
How did the loss of the Temple change the tradition's practice over the following centuries?

culture/kalinago.title: Kalinago
culture/kalinago.summary: The Kalinago, called Caribs by Europeans, are an Indigenous people of the Lesser Antilles who resisted colonization for nearly two centuries after Columbus, and today live mainly in the Kalinago Territory on Dominica.
facts: The Kalinago descend from earlier inhabitants of the Lesser Antilles and were there before Columbus reached the region in 1493.
They gained a reputation as effective resistance fighters, and their raids helped keep Europeans from permanent settlement on some islands for close to two centuries.
Dominica's mountainous volcanic interior gave them ground colonizers could not easily penetrate, and the island became a refuge for other Indigenous people fleeing colonization.
France claimed Dominica in 1635, but Kalinago resistance blocked permanent settlement for a time. Catholic missionaries arriving in 1642 recorded Kalinago language and life.
Kalinago raids on plantations on neighboring islands continued into the eighteenth century, and their descendants remain in the Kalinago Territory today.
culture/kalinago.context: The Kalinago inhabited the Caribbean and Atlantic World into the Early Modern Period, sharing the region with the Taino and resisting the disruptions of the Columbian Exchange longer than most neighbors. See War and Conflict.
culture/kalinago.observer: The Observer notes that difficult terrain, more than any single tactic, let one Caribbean people hold off colonization for two centuries after most of the region had fallen, then drew refugees from neighboring islands, making a stronghold a shared last refuge. Their presence today contradicts accounts that treat the Caribbean's Indigenous peoples as vanished. A specialist could argue that European rivalries left gaps in colonization as much as Kalinago strength did, which would weaken a reading that credits resistance alone.
questions: How much of the Kalinago's long resistance reflected their own strength versus European powers being divided or distracted?
How much pre-contact Kalinago culture survives on Dominica today, versus later adaptation?

culture/kanem-bornu-empire.title: Kanem-Bornu Empire
culture/kanem-bornu-empire.summary: Kanem-Bornu was a long-lived Muslim state around Lake Chad, governed by the Sayfawa dynasty, that survived by shifting its centre from Kanem to Bornu and lasted until 1893.
facts: Around 1396 the Bulala forced Mai Umar Idrismi to abandon Njimi and move the Kanembu people to Bornu, on the western side of Lake Chad. Over time intermarriage between the Kanembu and the peoples of Bornu produced a new people and language, the Kanuri.
With control of both capitals the Sayfawa dynasty became more powerful than before, and political authority came to rest in Bornu.

The empire peaked under Mai Idris Alooma (about 1571 to 1603), remembered for military skill, administrative reforms, and Islamic piety. He introduced legal and administrative reforms based on Islamic law, sponsored mosques, and made a pilgrimage to Mecca, where he set up a hostel for pilgrims from his empire.

His reforms and campaigns sustained the empire until the mid-17th century, when its power began to fade. In 1808 Fulani warriors conquered the capital, Ngazargamu. The Sayfawa dynasty ended in 1846 and the empire itself fell in 1893.
culture/kanem-bornu-empire.context: Kanem-Bornu was a neighbour of the Songhai Empire to the west and was overtaken in part by the Fulani movement associated with Usman dan Fodio and the Sokoto Caliphate.
culture/kanem-bornu-empire.observer: The Observer notes a state that survived an exile by moving its centre of gravity, and whose people fused with those who had displaced them into a new people. Where the political story-glue failed at one capital, the kin-lattice held it together long enough to build another.
questions: How is the earliest period of Kanem known, given that the sources consulted here say little about it?
How did Kanem-Bornu's rulers manage relations with the Fulani states that arose around 1808?

culture/kingdom-of-aksum.title: Kingdom of Aksum
culture/kingdom-of-aksum.summary: The Kingdom of Aksum was a trading empire in the highlands of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, from about the 1st to the 10th century CE.
facts: It controlled Red Sea trade between Rome, Arabia, and India.
It minted its own coins and built tall carved stone obelisks (stelae).
King Ezana adopted Christianity in the 4th century.
The Persian prophet Mani listed Aksum as one of the four great powers of his time, with Rome, Persia, and China.

culture/kingdom-of-benin.title: Kingdom of Benin
culture/kingdom-of-benin.summary: The Kingdom of Benin was a West African forest state of the Edo people, ruled by an oba from Benin City, that flourished from about the 13th century until British forces conquered it in 1897.
facts: The kingdom flourished from the 13th to the 19th century in the forest region of West Africa, in what is now southern Nigeria. In tradition, the Edo invited Prince Oranmiyan of Ife to rule in the 13th century, and his son Eweka became the first oba.

Under Oba Ewuare the Great (reigned about 1440 to 1480), the kingdom expanded and became highly organized, with guilds of craftsmen. He built up the army, rebuilt the royal compound, and gave Benin City moats and great walls.
In late December 1896 a party of nine British colonial officials led by James Robert Phillips set out for Benin City. On 4 January 1897 Edo chiefs ambushed and killed them near the village of Ugbine.

A British force of about 1,200 men under Sir Harry Rawson carried out the Benin Expedition from 9 to 18 February 1897. It occupied the capital after sustained resistance, burned parts of the city and palace, and removed large quantities of sacred and royal art.

The looted works, known as the Benin Bronzes, were sold to defray the costs of the expedition. Oba Ovonramwen was captured and exiled to Calabar, and the kingdom was incorporated into British Nigeria.
culture/kingdom-of-benin.context: The conquest of Benin belongs to the wider Scramble for Africa. The kingdom was also a contemporary of Kingdom of Kongo and traded with Europeans during the period of the Atlantic Slave Trade.
culture/kingdom-of-benin.observer: The Observer records a state's sacred and royal art taken by force and sold to pay for the force that took it. Where such objects are held is itself a claim about who may tell the story they carry, and the continuing argument over their display shows how long a seizure can outlast the event.
questions: What was the full scale of the destruction and loss of life in Benin City in 1897?
How should the sources on Benin's earlier centuries, which rest partly on oral tradition, be weighed against European accounts?

culture/kingdom-of-kongo.title: Kingdom of Kongo
culture/kingdom-of-kongo.summary: The Kingdom of Kongo was a centralized state in west-central Africa that adopted Catholic Christianity, dealt with Portugal as a diplomatic partner, and was drawn into the Atlantic slave trade. This note covers the documented period from Portuguese contact in 1483 to the defeat at Mbwila in 1665.
facts: Portuguese explorers reached the mouth of the Congo River in 1483. King Nzinga Nkuwu adopted Roman Catholicism, taking the name João I, and the capital was renamed São Salvador do Congo (Mbanza Kongo).

Afonso I (Nzinga Mbemba) ruled from 1506 to 1543. He won a brief civil war against his brother, centralized power at Mbanza Kongo, curbed the power of the nobility, and expanded the kingdom's borders through war.
Afonso I was raised a Christian, sent his son and others to Europe to be ordained as priests, and worked to convert his subjects.
From 1526 Afonso wrote a series of twenty-four letters to King João III of Portugal, appealing for an end to the slave trade.

At the Battle of Mbwila on 29 October 1665, Portuguese forces defeated the Kongo army and killed King António I. Kongo continued to exist, but from then on it no longer functioned as a unified kingdom.
culture/kingdom-of-kongo.context: Kongo was among the first African states to enter sustained diplomatic contact with Portugal, and its history is bound up with the Atlantic Slave Trade. It lay in a region long settled by Bantu-speaking peoples; see Bantu Expansion.
culture/kingdom-of-kongo.observer: The Observer notes a king who took up his visitors' meaning-engine and mark-code and used them to argue against the trade in his own people, while the exchange-web that consumed his subjects kept running. Adopting a partner's story-glue did not give the adopter control over the partner's demand.
questions: How far did Kongo's own rulers and elites take part in the slave trade, and how far did they resist it?
How much of Kongo's Christianity was imported, and how much was reshaped by Kongo's own traditions?

Later the capital moved to Meroe, a center of iron working.
Nubia has more pyramids than Egypt, though they are smaller.
The Meroitic script has been read phonetically but the language is not well understood.

culture/kingdom-of-mapungubwe.title: Kingdom of Mapungubwe
culture/kingdom-of-mapungubwe.summary: Mapungubwe was an Iron Age trading state at the meeting of the Limpopo and Shashe rivers in southern Africa, active from about the 11th to the 13th century, whose elite graves held gold and imported glass beads.
facts: The site lies at the confluence of the Limpopo and Shashe rivers. People settled at K2, near Bambandyanalo Hill, in the 11th century and had expanded to nearby Mapungubwe Hill by about 1220. From about 1220 to 1300 it was an advanced trading centre.
The Limpopo connected the region to the Indian Ocean ports, including Kilwa. Its people traded with Arabia, China, and India through East African harbours.
Glass beads, almost certainly from India, and fragments of Chinese celadon vessels show trade with states on the coast.
Some graves held bodies in the upright seated position associated with royalty, together with gold and copper objects and exotic glass beads.
The site was discovered in 1932 but was not widely publicized until much later. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage site in July 2003.
culture/kingdom-of-mapungubwe.context: Mapungubwe preceded Great Zimbabwe as a large regional centre and was linked into the Indian Ocean Trade Network through the Swahili Coast City-States.
culture/kingdom-of-mapungubwe.observer: The Observer notes that a hill in the interior of a continent, far from any coast, held beads made in India and dishes made in China. Status-signal travelled a long way to arrive on a chief's grave, and the trade that carried it left a clearer record than the state that received it.
questions: Why did Mapungubwe decline about the end of the 13th century, and did climate change play a part?
How did Mapungubwe's rulers relate to the later centres at Great Zimbabwe?

culture/kingdom-of-saba.title: Kingdom of Saba
culture/kingdom-of-saba.summary: Saba (Sheba) was an ancient South Arabian kingdom in what is now Yemen, centered on the city of Marib, and prosperous from the incense trade.
facts: Its earliest inscriptions date to about the 8th century BCE; some scholars propose an earlier origin, around 1000 BCE.
Marib was known for a great dam that irrigated the surrounding land, repaired several times before its final failure around the 6th century CE.
Sabaeans wrote in the South Arabian script.
The Queen of Sheba appears in the Hebrew Bible and the Quran; her historicity is not established.
The neighboring kingdom of Himyar absorbed Saba around 275 CE.
culture/kingdom-of-saba.context: Saba's wealth came from the Incense Trade, which connected southern Arabia with the Mediterranean. It sits in the Arabian Peninsula alongside the Nabataeans of the north. Kingdom of Saba sits in the Iron Age and the region Arabian Peninsula, and belongs to the theme thread of Trade and Economy and Language and Writing.
culture/kingdom-of-saba.observer: The Observer notes that the best-known image of Saba, a queen visiting a king, comes from religious texts written elsewhere, while its own inscriptions record dams, temples, and commerce. The outside story shapes memory more than the inside record.
questions: When did the kingdom form, and how far did it extend?

culture/kushan-empire.title: Kushan Empire
culture/kushan-empire.summary: The Kushan Empire, from about 30 to 375 CE, was a Central Asian empire spanning Bactria and northern India that controlled key Silk Road routes and patronized Buddhism.
facts: It grew from the Yuezhi confederation and was consolidated by Kujula Kadphises around 30 CE.
Kanishka, whose reign dates are uncertain, is remembered as a patron of Buddhism.
Gandhara art, which blended Greek and Indian styles, produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form.
Kushan coins bore deities from Greek, Iranian, and Indian traditions.
The empire connected Rome, Parthia, India, and Han China commercially.
culture/kushan-empire.context: The Kushans occupied the crossroads of the Opening of the Silk Roads and carried the traditions of Siddhartha Gautama eastward. They ruled where the Han Dynasty and Indian states met.
