culture/lakota.title: Lakota
culture/lakota.summary: The Lakota, or Teton Sioux, are the western division of the Oceti Sakowin, the Seven Council Fires. From the 1700s they built a mounted bison-hunting society on the northern Great Plains, broken by United States force by 1890.
facts: The Lakota form seven divisions, among them the Oglala and Hunkpapa.
Most historians say the Lakota moved west from Minnesota, reaching the Black Hills between the 1770s and 1820s; Lakota tradition places their origin there.
The Lakota obtained horses from the Cheyenne between about 1700 and 1730, becoming mounted bison hunters who gathered each summer.
Lakota bands were extended families (tiospaye); akicita societies policed camps and hunts.

The 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty set the Black Hills aside within the Great Sioux Reservation. Lakota and allies destroyed Custer's command in 1876, and the United States seized the Hills in 1877; in 1980 the Supreme Court held this taking required compensation.
With bison nearly gone by the 1880s, soldiers killed an estimated 250 to 300 Lakota at Wounded Knee on 29 December 1890.
culture/lakota.context: The Lakota flourished in North America during the Industrial Age, on horses from the Columbian Exchange; Sitting Bull was a Hunkpapa leader. See War and Conflict, Trade and Economy and Kinship and Society.
culture/lakota.observer: The Observer notes that the Lakota linked scattered bands through a kin-lattice and a shared summer gathering, and made the imported horse a tool-lineage. Their claim-line rested on use and treaty, and the Black Hills still carry a meaning-engine's weight, shown by the Lakota refusal of the 1980 award. A specialist could argue that the bands often acted apart and that Lakota power was regional and brief, which would weaken a lasting kin-lattice reading.
questions: When did the Lakota cross the Missouri, and how do winter counts and emergence accounts fit the record?
How far did smallpox among Missouri villages, not Lakota strength alone, drive Lakota expansion?

culture/lapita-culture.title: Lapita Culture
culture/lapita-culture.summary: The Lapita culture was a seafaring society that appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago around 1600 BCE and spread rapidly east through the western Pacific, and its people were ancestors of the Polynesians.
facts: Lapita is identified by pottery decorated with fine stamped geometric patterns.
Sites spread from the Bismarck Archipelago to Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa by roughly 1000 to 800 BCE.
Lapita people moved obsidian and other goods over long distances.
Ancient DNA from the Teouma cemetery in Vanuatu shows the first settlers there had ancestry related to East Asians; later, Papuan ancestry became dominant in Vanuatu.
Lapita descendants settled Polynesia in later centuries.
culture/lapita-culture.context: The Lapita were the Pacific arm of the Austronesian Expansion and the direct ancestors of the Polynesians. Their voyages set the stage for the Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific. Lapita Culture sits in the Bronze Age and the region Oceania, and belongs to the theme thread of Trade and Economy and Art and Ritual.
culture/lapita-culture.observer: The Observer notes that the culture is defined almost entirely by pots, yet the pots record boats: a sailing tradition that crossed hundreds of kilometers of open ocean. The material that survives tells the story of what did not.
questions: What drove the rapid expansion into previously uninhabited islands?

culture/majapahit.title: Majapahit
culture/majapahit.summary: Majapahit was a Hindu-Buddhist empire based in eastern Java, founded in 1293 after the Yuan dynasty's failed invasion of Java, and dominant in the Indonesian archipelago in the 14th century.
facts: Raden Wijaya founded the kingdom in 1293, after helping Mongol forces defeat a rival and then turning against them.
It reached its height under Hayam Wuruk with his minister Gajah Mada in the mid-14th century.
The court poem Nagarakretagama, written in 1365, lists many regions as dependencies.
How far actual control extended is debated.
Its power declined in the 15th and 16th centuries as Islamic port-sultanates grew.
culture/majapahit.context: Majapahit followed Srivijaya as the main power of the archipelago and repelled the naval expedition of the Mongol Conquests. It profited from the Indian Ocean Trade Network. Majapahit sits in the Medieval Period and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Trade and Economy and War and Conflict.
culture/majapahit.observer: The Observer notes that modern Indonesia invokes Majapahit as a precedent for an archipelagic state, though the empire's actual reach is uncertain. States often choose their ancestors and then enlarge them.
questions: How much of the archipelago did Majapahit truly control?

culture/mal-ta-and-the-ancient-north-eur.title: Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians
culture/mal-ta-and-the-ancient-north-eur.summary: The Mal'ta boy, a child who lived near Lake Baikal about 24,000 years ago, has a genome that revealed a previously unknown population of 'Ancient North Eurasians' who contributed to the ancestry of both Europeans and Native Americans.
facts: The remains were excavated at Mal'ta in Siberia in the 1920s and their genome was sequenced in 2013.
It was then the oldest modern human genome published.
Between about 14 and 38 percent of the boy's genome is shared with present-day Native Americans, in different estimates.
The result showed that Native American ancestry has two roots: East Asian and Ancient North Eurasian.
culture/mal-ta-and-the-ancient-north-eur.context: The finding reshaped the Peopling of the Americas, which occurred around the Last Glacial Maximum. See Siberia and the Arctic.
culture/mal-ta-and-the-ancient-north-eur.observer: The Observer notes that a single child's bones, buried with ornaments, spoke across 24,000 years to a question about the far side of the world. The past holds its answers in unexpected places.
questions: How did Ancient North Eurasian ancestry spread across continents?

culture/malacca-sultanate.title: Malacca Sultanate
culture/malacca-sultanate.summary: The Malacca (Melaka) Sultanate was a Malay port state on the Strait of Malacca, founded about 1400, that became the leading trading port of Southeast Asia in the 15th century and helped spread Islam through the archipelago before the Portuguese took it in 1511.
facts: Parameswara, a half-Javanese nobleman from Palembang in Sumatra, established the kingdom of Melaka about 1400 after trying to establish himself at Temasik (Singapore).

According to tradition, Parameswara married the daughter of a Muslim ruler and converted to Islam, taking the name Iskandar and the title of sultan. Melaka became instrumental in the spread of Islam through the Malay world.
It grew into the most important port in Southeast Asia in the 15th and early 16th century, an entrepôt through which flowed silks, spices, and porcelain, as well as local tin.

The Portuguese, unable to negotiate a friendly trading arrangement, invaded the city in 1511 and forced the sultan to flee. The fall of Melaka marked the beginning of European colonial power in the region.
culture/malacca-sultanate.context: Malacca inherited the role of the older maritime empire of Srivijaya and competed with the Majapahit state of Java. It sat at the centre of the Indian Ocean Trade Network, and its capture followed the arrival of the Portuguese Sea Route to India.
culture/malacca-sultanate.observer: The Observer notes a port that was valuable because it sat on a strait, and a ruling house that took on a new meaning-engine in a way that also suited its trade. The Portuguese seizure in 1511 shows an exchange-web being captured at its narrowest point.
questions: How much of the conversion story rests on later Malay tradition, and how much on contemporary records?
How large was Melaka's population, and how did it manage so many merchant communities?

Oral tradition records the epic of Sundiata, told by griots.
The rulers were Muslim, and scholarship flourished in cities such as Timbuktu.
Its power declined from the 15th century as the Songhai Empire rose.

culture/manichaeism.title: Manichaeism
culture/manichaeism.summary: Manichaeism was a dualistic religion founded in third-century Persia by Mani, teaching a cosmic struggle between light and darkness. It spread from North Africa to China within four centuries and died out under persecution by the 14th century.
facts: Mani, born about 216 CE in the Persian Empire, called himself the Apostle of Light and taught that the material world imprisons divine light in darkness, with salvation lying in freeing that light.
He drew on Zoroastrian, Christian, Buddhist and Gnostic ideas and presented himself as the final prophet after Jesus and the Buddha.
The religion spread from Roman North Africa to Central Asia and China, helped by trade routes. A missionary reached the Tang court in 694, and freedom of worship followed in 732.
In 296 the emperor Diocletian ordered Manichaean leaders burned with their scriptures, and Roman and Persian persecution largely ended the faith in the west by the sixth century.
In China the anti-Buddhist persecution of 843 also seized Manichaean property and executed clergy, and the religion faded into Buddhism and Daoism by the 14th century.
culture/manichaeism.context: Manichaeism arose in Mesopotamia during Classical Antiquity, within the Sasanian Empire (not yet a vault note), drawing on ideas shared with Zoroastrianism before spreading as far as the Tang Dynasty's China. See Religion and Belief.
culture/manichaeism.observer: The Observer notes that a meaning-engine assembled from older traditions crossed Eurasia in four centuries along trade routes, then was suppressed by Roman, Persian and Chinese states, each for its own stated reasons. It survived roughly a thousand years under official persecution nearly everywhere it took root. A specialist could argue that its decline in China reflects absorption into Buddhism and Daoism as much as suppression, which would weaken a reading of persecution as the sole cause of its extinction.
questions: How much of Manichaeism's decline in China was suppression versus absorption into other traditions?
How consistent was Manichaean teaching across regions as different as Rome, Persia and China?

culture/maori.title: Maori
culture/maori.summary: The Maori are the Polynesian people of Aotearoa (New Zealand), who settled the islands around 1250 to 1300 CE and developed a distinct culture and language.
facts: Radiocarbon dating suggests the first settlement of New Zealand was around 1250 to 1300 CE.
The giant flightless moa was hunted to extinction within roughly a century or two of settlement.
Maori society was organized around kin groups (whanau, hapu, and iwi).
The Treaty of Waitangi was signed with the British Crown in 1840; disputes over its meaning continue.
Te reo Maori became an official language of New Zealand in 1987.
culture/maori.context: The Maori were the last major landmass settlers in the Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific. Their relationship with the British Crown is defined by the Treaty of Waitangi. Maori sits in the Medieval Period and the region Oceania, and belongs to the theme thread of Kinship and Society and Language and Writing.
culture/maori.observer: The Observer notes that the last large habitable landmass on Earth was settled by boat only about 750 years ago, well within historical time. That a people arrived so late, and remembered the voyage, makes their genealogies unusually precise records of migration.
questions: Where in Polynesia did the settlers come from?

culture/mapuche.title: Mapuche
culture/mapuche.summary: The Mapuche are the Indigenous people of south-central Chile and Argentina, who resisted both the Inca and the Spanish and kept their independence for centuries.
facts: According to Spanish chroniclers, the Mapuche halted the Inca advance at the Maule River in the late 15th century.
The Arauco War with Spain ran from about 1546 to 1662 and was nicknamed the 'Indian Flanders'.
By the Parliament of Quillin in 1641, Spain recognized the Bio-Bio river as a border and agreed to withdraw to its north.
Chile's Occupation of the Araucania (1861 to 1883) incorporated Mapuche territory; sources cite that the Mapuche lost most of their land and were confined to reservations.
culture/mapuche.context: The Mapuche lived south of the reach of the Inca Empire and the Spanish empire after the Columbian Exchange, keeping political autonomy longer than most.
culture/mapuche.observer: The Observer notes a people that negotiated as a sovereign party with a global empire, on the ground of a treaty, for over two centuries. The record of Indigenous diplomacy is longer than colonial narratives often suggest.
questions: How did the Mapuche organize their military and political life?

culture/marajoara-culture.title: Marajoara Culture
culture/marajoara-culture.summary: The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajo Island at the mouth of the Amazon, known for large earthen mounds and richly decorated ceramics, with its ceramic tradition dated about 400 to 1300 CE.
facts: Marajo Island is roughly the size of Switzerland, and mound building there began around 300 CE.
Mounds reach up to about 20 meters in height, and the largest multi-mound sites may have housed several thousand people.
Ceramics include burial urns, figurines, and elaborately painted and incised vessels, suggesting specialized craft production.
The mounds were largely abandoned by about 1350 CE.
culture/marajoara-culture.context: See Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths. Scholars have debated whether the mound-building Marajoara were a complex chiefdom sustained without intensive farming.
culture/marajoara-culture.observer: The Observer notes that the Marajoara raised their own hills on a seasonally flooded plain. Building earth up was a way of making living space where there was none.
questions: Were the Marajoara chiefdoms, or something more complex?

Maya writing combines signs for words and syllables and is largely deciphered.
They kept precise calendars and used the concept of zero.

culture/minoans.title: Minoans
culture/minoans.summary: The Minoans were a Bronze Age maritime civilization on the island of Crete, known for palaces such as Knossos and vivid frescoes. Their palatial culture flourished from about 2000 BCE until about 1450 BCE.
facts: They traded across the eastern Mediterranean, and their cultural influence reached Egypt, Cyprus, Canaan, and Anatolia.
They used scripts, Linear A and Cretan hieroglyphs, that have not been deciphered. Linear B, adapted from Linear A, records Mycenaean Greek and was deciphered in 1952.

The eruption of the Thera volcano damaged settlements in the Aegean. Radiocarbon dates put it around 1600 BCE, while links with Egyptian chronology suggest about 1500 BCE. The century-long gap is unresolved.

Around 1450 BCE, Mycenaean Greeks became dominant on Crete and Linear B was used at Knossos. Scholars debate whether this was a conquest or a gradual absorption. Knossos remained a palace centre after the other Minoan palaces declined, until its own destruction some time later.
culture/minoans.context: The Minoans are part of the Mediterranean Basin trading world that collapsed in the Bronze Age Collapse.
culture/minoans.observer: The Observer notes a culture known mainly through images of bull-leaping and sea life, since its writing cannot yet be read. What survives shapes how a culture is remembered.
questions: Can Linear A be deciphered?

culture/mississippian-culture.title: Mississippian Culture
culture/mississippian-culture.summary: The Mississippian culture was a family of Native American societies that farmed maize and built platform mounds across the Midwest and Southeast, from about 800 or 1000 to 1600 CE, with Cahokia as its largest town.
facts: Mississippian communities farmed river floodplains, growing maize with beans, squash, and older native crops.
Hereditary chiefs ruled from platform mounds carrying their houses or temples.
Cahokia grew rapidly from about 1050 to perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people. Its Mound 72 held about 270 burials, including mass graves of mostly young women, interpreted as sacrifices.
Shell gorgets and copper plates showing bird-warrior imagery, called the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex, circulated among centers from roughly 1100 or 1200.

Cahokia declined from about 1200 and was largely abandoned by roughly 1350 to 1450, amid drought, flooding, and social strain. After Hernando de Soto's 1539 expedition, disease, warfare, and slave raiding helped end the remaining chiefdoms by about 1730.
culture/mississippian-culture.context: The Mississippian culture flourished in North America during the Medieval Period, farming maize domesticated in Mesoamerica (Domestication of Maize), with its largest town at Cahokia. Mississippian towns overlapped in time with the Ancestral Puebloans and later faced the Columbian Exchange. See Religion and Belief and Trade and Economy.
culture/mississippian-culture.observer: Mississippian towns were bound less by one state than by a shared meaning-engine, its imagery carried on shell and copper status-signals through an exchange-web. Chiefly families marked claim-lines with mounds, and Mound 72's mass graves, if read as sacrifice, show sanctioned harm within a grief-rite; earthworks and living Native nations survive. A specialist could argue that the shared imagery reflects parallel local choices more than one connected tradition, which would weaken the reading of a single meaning-engine.

How much did drought, warfare, and European disease each contribute to Mississippian decline?

The empire ran a relay postal system (the yam) that sped communication across Eurasia.
It promoted trade and tolerated many religions.

culture/muisca.title: Muisca
culture/muisca.summary: The Muisca were the peoples of the Colombian highlands around present-day Bogota, organized in a loose confederation of rulers, whose gold ritual inspired the legend of El Dorado.
facts: The main rulers were the zipa of Bacata, the zaque of Hunza, the iraca of Sugamuxi, and the ruler of Tundama.

Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada led a Spanish expedition from Santa Marta in April 1536 with roughly 800 to 900 Spaniards, together with native carriers and enslaved Africans. Nearly three-quarters of the Spaniards died, mostly from illness and hunger; one scholarly account counts 179 survivors.
The Spanish conquest of the Muisca took place from 1537 to 1540.
According to legend, a Muisca ruler covered himself in gold dust and dived into Lake Guatavita; the Spanish found emeralds rather than golden cities.
culture/muisca.context: The Muisca lived in the northern Andes, outside the Inca Empire. Their fall is part of the Columbian Exchange era of conquest.
culture/muisca.observer: The Observer notes that a ritual was turned into a myth of a golden city, and that the myth then drove real expeditions. A story about a place can send armies to it.
questions: When did the Muisca confederation form?

culture/mycenaean-greeks.title: Mycenaean Greeks
culture/mycenaean-greeks.summary: The Mycenaeans were the Bronze Age Greek-speaking civilization of mainland Greece, centered on palace-fortresses such as Mycenae, Tiryns, and Pylos, from about 1600 to 1100 BCE.
facts: Their administrative records were written in Linear B, an early form of Greek, on clay tablets.
Michael Ventris deciphered Linear B in 1952, with help from John Chadwick.
Shaft graves at Mycenae, dated to about 1600 BCE, held gold masks and weapons; Heinrich Schliemann excavated them in 1876.
The Mycenaeans took over or influenced the Minoan palace at Knossos on Crete by about 1450 BCE.
Their palace system collapsed around 1200 to 1100 BCE.
culture/mycenaean-greeks.context: The Mycenaeans inherited much of the Minoans' maritime trade and artistic style, and their palace economies fell in the Bronze Age Collapse. Later Ancient Greeks preserved memory of them in epic poetry. Mycenaean Greeks sits in the Bronze Age and the region Mediterranean Basin, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Language and Writing and Trade and Economy.
culture/mycenaean-greeks.observer: The Observer notes that the earliest Greek writing is an inventory of goods, not poetry. Writing began as bookkeeping for palaces, then was lost with the palaces, and was reinvented centuries later as an alphabet.
questions: What caused the palaces to fall: invasion, earthquakes, internal conflict, or wider disruption?

culture/nabataeans.title: Nabataeans
culture/nabataeans.summary: The Nabataeans were an Arab people who controlled caravan routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean from the 4th century BCE, building Petra and Hegra, until Rome annexed their kingdom in 106 CE.
facts: They are first mentioned in Greek sources in 312 BCE.
Petra, in present-day Jordan, has tombs and temples cut into sandstone cliffs, and an elaborate system of water channels and cisterns.
Hegra (Mada'in Salih) in northwestern Saudi Arabia has similar rock-cut tombs and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2008.
The Nabataean script is widely considered an ancestor of the Arabic script.
The Roman emperor Trajan annexed the kingdom in 106 CE.
culture/nabataeans.context: The Nabataeans controlled a major part of the Incense Trade and were absorbed by Rome. Nabataeans sits in the Classical Antiquity and the region Arabian Peninsula, and belongs to the theme thread of Trade and Economy and Art and Ritual.
culture/nabataeans.observer: The Observer notes that the Nabataeans built monuments in rock, where they could not be moved, on a trade based on goods that moved constantly. Their rock-cut tombs preserved their name while the caravans left no trace.
questions: How did the Nabataean script develop into Arabic?

culture/neo-assyrian-empire.title: Neo-Assyrian Empire
culture/neo-assyrian-empire.summary: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, from about 911 to 609 BCE, was a large empire based in northern Mesopotamia, known for its army, its palace reliefs, and the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh.
facts: Its main capitals were Ashur, Kalhu (Nimrud), Dur-Sharrukin, and Nineveh.
At its height in the 7th century BCE it controlled Mesopotamia, the Levant, and, briefly, Egypt.
It used mass deportation to move conquered populations across the empire.
The library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh held tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments, including a standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh.
A coalition of Babylonians and Medes captured Nineveh in 612 BCE, and Assyrian resistance ended by about 609 BCE.
culture/neo-assyrian-empire.context: The Neo-Assyrian Empire continued the cuneiform tradition begun by the Sumerians and preserved much of it in royal libraries. It is an early example of a state organized around Sanctioned Harm, as described in its own propaganda. Neo-Assyrian Empire sits in the Iron Age and the region Mesopotamia, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Language and Writing.
culture/neo-assyrian-empire.observer: The Observer notes that the empire boasted of its violence in stone reliefs and also collected and copied the literature of its predecessors. A state can be both a destroyer and an archivist, and the archive is why we know about the destruction.
questions: How reliable are Assyrian royal inscriptions about their own campaigns?

culture/norse.title: Norse
culture/norse.summary: The Norse (Vikings) were seafaring peoples from Scandinavia who raided, traded, and settled across Europe and the North Atlantic, from about 793 to 1066 CE.
facts: The raid on Lindisfarne monastery in 793 is often taken as the start of the Viking Age.
Norse settlers colonized Iceland (from about 870) and Greenland (from about 985).
They reached North America; the L'Anse aux Meadows site in Newfoundland has been dated by tree rings to 1021 CE.
Norse traders also traveled the rivers of eastern Europe, exchanging goods for silver from the Islamic world.
culture/norse.context: The Norse connected Europe to the North Atlantic and to the Eurasian exchange-web.
culture/norse.observer: The Observer notes that raiders and traders were often the same people, with the balance of violence and commerce depending on the opportunity.
questions: Why did Norse Greenland disappear?

culture/olmecs.title: Olmecs
culture/olmecs.summary: The Olmecs were an early Mesoamerican culture on the Gulf coast of Mexico, best known for colossal carved stone heads, from about 1200 to 400 BCE.
facts: Major centers included San Lorenzo and La Venta.
Colossal heads, some over 3 meters tall, were carved from basalt hauled long distances.

They worked rubber. The name 'Olmec' is the Nahuatl word for 'rubber people', which the Aztecs applied to later Gulf-lowland neighbors and which archaeologists later applied to this ancient culture; its own name is unknown.
Whether they were a 'mother culture' or one of several interacting societies is debated.
culture/olmecs.context: The Olmecs are among the earliest societies in Mesoamerica and influenced later cultures such as the Maya.
culture/olmecs.observer: The Observer sees a case of monumental art as a status-signal for rulers, in a region with no metal tools and no wheeled transport.
questions: Did the Olmecs have writing?

culture/ottoman-empire.title: Ottoman Empire
culture/ottoman-empire.summary: The Ottoman Empire was a state founded in Anatolia about 1299 that grew into a multiethnic empire across Southeast Europe, West Asia, and North Africa, lasting until 1922.
facts: Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453.
The empire peaked under Suleiman the Magnificent (reigned 1520 to 1566).
The millet system gave religious communities a degree of self-government.
The sultanate was abolished in 1922, and the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed in 1923.
culture/ottoman-empire.context: See Constantinople. The empire inherited earlier states such as the Abbasid Caliphate and lasted into the Industrial Age.
culture/ottoman-empire.observer: The Observer notes a long-lived empire that governed diverse peoples by layering communities. Pluralism was a practical answer to the problem of ruling strangers.
questions: How did the millet system work in practice?

culture/pagan-kingdom.title: Pagan Kingdom
culture/pagan-kingdom.summary: The Pagan Kingdom united the Irrawaddy valley in what is now Myanmar under King Anawrahta and his successors, made Theravada Buddhism its state religion, and built thousands of temples at Bagan before falling to the Mongols in 1287.
facts: Anawrahta reigned from 11 August 1044 to 11 April 1077. He founded the Pagan Empire in the 1050s and 1060s, apparently unifying the Irrawaddy valley and its edges for the first time.

Anawrahta was converted to Theravada Buddhism by a Mon monk, Shin Arahan. The Mon royal family, scholars, and craftsmen were brought to Pagan, and a form of Theravada adopted from Sri Lanka became official around 1056.
Pagan's rulers built more than 10,000 Buddhist temples in the Bagan Archaeological Zone, of which more than 2,000 survive.
Mongol armies invaded from 1277 to 1287. Pagan's rule ended in 1287, and Myinsaing took over on 17 December 1287.
culture/pagan-kingdom.context: Pagan was a contemporary of the Khmer Empire at Angkor to the east, and its end came through the Mongol Conquests.
culture/pagan-kingdom.observer: The Observer notes a ruler who used one shared meaning-engine to bind a population, and a building programme so large that the surviving remnant of it still fills a plain. Status-signal was directed upward at the divine, and the result outlasted the state that paid for it.
questions: How much of the Mongol effect on Pagan was military destruction, and how much was the state's own weakness before 1277?
How were more than 10,000 temples financed and maintained?

culture/phoenicians.title: Phoenicians
culture/phoenicians.summary: The Phoenicians were seafaring traders from city-states on the Levant coast (such as Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos) who founded colonies across the Mediterranean.
facts: They founded Carthage, traditionally in 814 BCE.
They spread a simple alphabet of about 22 letters.
They were known for purple dye and for shipbuilding.
Few Phoenician writings survive; most of what is known comes from others.
culture/phoenicians.context: The Phoenicians linked the Mediterranean Basin by sea and spread the Alphabet after the Bronze Age Collapse.
culture/phoenicians.observer: The Observer notes a network of commercial city-states rather than a territorial empire, an example of an exchange-web that carries a technology further than any army.

culture/polynesians.title: Polynesians
culture/polynesians.summary: Polynesians are the Austronesian-speaking peoples of the central and eastern Pacific, who developed long-range voyaging and settled the islands from Hawai'i to Aotearoa and Rapa Nui.
facts: Ancestors of Polynesians, the Lapita people, spread through Near Oceania and reached Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa between about 1300 and 900 BCE.
Voyagers used double-hulled canoes and non-instrument navigation.
Societies ranged from chiefdoms to kingdoms, such as in Hawai'i and Tonga.
Rapa Nui (Easter Island) is known for its large stone statues (moai).

culture/qing-dynasty.title: Qing Dynasty
culture/qing-dynasty.summary: The Qing dynasty (1644 to 1912) was the last imperial dynasty of China, founded by the Manchus after they overthrew the Ming, and it expanded China's borders to their largest extent.
facts: The Qing extended control over Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang.
Population and the economy grew strongly in the 18th century.
The dynasty faced the Opium Wars, the Taiping Rebellion, and the Boxer Rebellion in the 19th century.
The last emperor, Puyi, abdicated in February 1912.
culture/qing-dynasty.context: The Qing followed the Ming Dynasty and ended with the 1911 revolution. See East Asia.
culture/qing-dynasty.observer: The Observer notes a dynasty of outsiders who ruled by adopting the forms of the ruled: Manchu rulers governed through Confucian institutions. Ruling a large population often means adopting its ways.
questions: How Chinese, and how Manchu, was Qing rule?

The empire built roads, aqueducts, and cities, and developed law and engineering, including concrete.
Citizenship was extended to nearly all free inhabitants in 212 CE.
The Roman world was tied together by Latin and Greek, and by trade.

culture/safavid-empire.title: Safavid Empire
culture/safavid-empire.summary: The Safavid Empire (1501 to 1736) was a Persian dynasty that made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran and ruled from Tabriz and later Isfahan.
facts: Ismail I proclaimed himself shah at Tabriz in 1501 and imposed Twelver Shia Islam.
The Ottomans defeated Safavid forces at Chaldiran in 1514.
Abbas I (r. 1588 to 1629) moved the capital to Isfahan and rebuilt the empire's army and economy.
Isfahan became known for its mosques, squares, and gardens.
The Safavid state collapsed after an Afghan invasion in 1722 and ended in 1736.

Safavid Empire sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Iranian Plateau, and belongs to the theme thread of Religion and Belief and War and Conflict and Art and Ritual.
culture/safavid-empire.observer: The Observer notes that Iran's largely Shia identity today can be traced to the deliberate policy of one dynasty. A meaning-engine can be adopted by state decision within a few decades and then treated as ancient.
questions: How quickly did the population convert to Shia Islam?

culture/scythians.title: Scythians
culture/scythians.summary: 'Scythian' is a general name for the horse-riding nomads who lived across the Eurasian steppe in the Iron Age, from about the 9th to the 3rd century BCE, known from Greek writers and rich burial mounds.
facts: Herodotus (5th century BCE) described Scythian customs, including burial rites and warfare.
The royal mound Arzhan 1 in Tuva dates to the late 9th century BCE; Arzhan 2 held about 5,600 gold objects, including a cloak studded with some 2,500 gold panthers.
Frozen tombs at Pazyryk in the Altai, of the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE, preserved textiles, tattoos, and horse gear.
The Scythians lived by herding horses, sheep, and cattle, moving with the seasons.
culture/scythians.context: The Scythians interacted with the Achaemenid Persians and the Greeks. See Central Asian Steppe and Siberia and the Arctic.
culture/scythians.observer: The Observer notes a people who left almost no writing of their own, yet whose art in gold and felt survives at extraordinary quality. Their story reaches us largely through outsiders' texts and their own graves.
questions: How connected were the far-flung 'Scythian' groups?

culture/shang-dynasty.title: Shang Dynasty
culture/shang-dynasty.summary: The Shang dynasty was the earliest Chinese dynasty with written records, ruling parts of the Yellow River region from about 1600 to 1046 BCE.
facts: Divination inscribed on oracle bones is the earliest securely attested Chinese writing (about 1250 BCE).
Elite tombs contain bronze ritual vessels and evidence of human sacrifice.
The late capital was at Yin, near modern Anyang.
The Shang were overthrown by the Zhou.
culture/shang-dynasty.context: See Invention of Writing. The Shang is a foundation of the tradition that leads to the Han Dynasty.
culture/shang-dynasty.observer: The Observer notes that the first Chinese writing was used to ask questions of ancestors. Writing here began as a channel to the dead rather than to accountants.
questions: How centralized was Shang rule?

culture/shinto.title: Shinto
culture/shinto.summary: Shinto is the indigenous religious tradition of Japan, centered on kami, a broad category of spirits, deified ancestors and natural forces, with no single founder or scripture and a long history of local shrine practice.
facts: Its practices trace to communal rites of purification, offering and harmony with nature among agricultural communities of the Yayoi period, roughly 300 BCE to 300 CE, with no founder or original canonical text.
Kami covers gods, spirits, deified people, ancestors and natural phenomena, worshipped through offerings and ritual at shrines.
By 1945 Japan had 218 national shrines and about 110,000 local ones.

From 1882 State Shinto held the emperor to be descended from the sun goddess Amaterasu and demanded loyalty on that basis, until the Allied occupation's 1945 Shinto Directive ended state sponsorship and the emperor renounced claims to divinity.
Only 3 to 4 million people worldwide formally identify as Shinto, though many in Japan take part in its rites alongside Buddhism.
culture/shinto.context: Shinto developed in East Asia in Japan during the Iron Age with no single founding date. It was mobilized as State Shinto around the reign of Emperor Meiji and lost state sponsorship after World War II. See Religion and Belief.
culture/shinto.observer: The Observer notes that a diffuse tradition of local shrine practice was gathered in the late nineteenth century and pointed at one claim, the emperor's divine descent, turning scattered story-glue into a tool of the state that occupying powers dismantled in a single directive. Few people formally name Shinto their religion, yet many join its shrine rites, so identification counts little of the practice. A specialist could argue that participation, not adherent counts, measures the tradition, which would weaken any reading of its reach from identification numbers alone.
questions: How much does formal identification undercount actual participation in Shinto practice?
How much of today's shrine practice descends from before the State Shinto period?

culture/sikhism.title: Sikhism
culture/sikhism.summary: Sikhism began in the Punjab region of South Asia with the teaching of Guru Nanak, born in 1469, and developed through a line of ten human teachers into a monotheistic tradition with its own scripture and, since 1699, a formal order of initiated members called the Khalsa.
facts: Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539) taught belief in one God, social equality across caste lines, and rejection of ritualism, gathering the first Sikh community in Punjab.
Nine more teachers followed him, together the Ten Gurus, regarded by Sikhs as sharing one continuous spirit of guidance.
In 1699 the tenth guru, Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa, a discipline of initiated Sikhs marked by the Five Ks, articles of faith including uncut hair, organized in part to defend the faith.

Before his death, Gobind Singh declared that Sikhs should treat their scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, a compilation of hymns by the gurus and other spiritual figures, as their living guru, ending the line of human gurus.
About 25 to 30 million Sikhs live today, mostly in Punjab, India, where they form a majority of the region's population, with further communities across the global Sikh diaspora.
culture/sikhism.context: Sikhism arose in South Asia during the Medieval Period, within the Punjab region later ruled in part by the Mughal Empire. See Religion and Belief.
culture/sikhism.observer: The Observer notes that when the line of living teachers ended in 1699, the community shifted memory-outsourcing onto a book, declaring a text itself a guru, an unusual solution other traditions solve through institutions or bloodlines. The Khalsa also shows a meaning-engine adopting sanctioned self-defense as part of its identity in response to persecution. A specialist could argue that ending the line of human gurus reflected particular circumstances of Gobind Singh's own time as much as settled theology, which would weaken a reading of it as inevitable.
questions: How did the decision to end the line of human gurus shape the community's later development?
How much of the Khalsa's military character reflects a response to specific persecution versus an intended permanent feature of the faith?

culture/sintashta-culture.title: Sintashta Culture
culture/sintashta-culture.summary: The Sintashta culture was a Bronze Age society of the southern Urals steppe, from about 2100 to 1800 BCE, known for fortified settlements and the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots.
facts: About 20 or more fortified settlements are known, including Sintashta and Arkaim, with concentric walls, ditches, and towers.
Elite graves contain horses, weapons, and chariots with spoked wheels dated to about 2000 BCE.
The culture is often linked, though not conclusively, to speakers of early Indo-Iranian languages.
Chariot warfare later spread across Eurasia.
culture/sintashta-culture.context: See The Wheel and Indo-European Language Spread. The Sintashta may have contributed to chariot use in Central Asian Steppe and Near Eastern warfare.
culture/sintashta-culture.observer: The Observer notes a culture of walled villages and elite horse burials, a sign that violence and prestige were entangled with a new technology.
questions: What was the Sintashta's relationship to later Indo-Iranian peoples?

culture/sogdians.title: Sogdians
culture/sogdians.summary: The Sogdians were an Iranian-speaking people of the Central Asian oases (Samarkand, Bukhara, Panjikent) who became the leading merchants of the Silk Roads from about the 4th century CE.
facts: They built trading colonies from Central Asia to China, acting as caravan leaders, interpreters, and bankers.
Their language served as a lingua franca along the Silk Roads and as a court language of the First Turkic Khaganate.
The 'Ancient Letters' of about 313 CE, found in a Great Wall tower, show Sogdian colonies writing to the home base in Samarkand.
Sogdians helped spread Buddhism, Manichaeism, and later other religions across Asia.
culture/sogdians.context: The Sogdians carried the Opening of the Silk Roads trade through Samarkand and served Tang Dynasty China and the Turkic khaganates.
culture/sogdians.observer: The Observer notes that a people who never built a large empire shaped the economy of Eurasia. Merchants who speak many languages can be more influential than rulers who speak one.
questions: How did Sogdian merchant communities organize credit and trust?

culture/sokoto-caliphate.title: Sokoto Caliphate
culture/sokoto-caliphate.summary: The Sokoto Caliphate was an Islamic state in what is now northern Nigeria, founded through the jihad of Usman dan Fodio from 1804, and the largest state in West Africa in the 19th century.
facts: The jihad began in February 1804 and lasted until about 1808; by 1815 the caliphate included most of northern Nigeria and parts of Cameroon and Niger.
Some estimates give the caliphate 10 to 20 million people by the 1830s, making it very populous.
It was a center of scholarship and of trade across the Sahel.
British forces conquered it in 1903.

culture/sokoto-caliphate.observer: The Observer notes a state founded by a scholar and a reformer, who wrote extensively as well as fought. The caliphate produced a large body of writing in Arabic, Hausa, and Fulfulde.
questions: How centralized was the caliphate's rule?

culture/song-dynasty.title: Song Dynasty
culture/song-dynasty.summary: The Song dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279 CE and presided over major advances in commerce, technology, and urban life.
facts: It issued some of the world's first government paper money.
Cities such as Kaifeng and Hangzhou were among the largest in the world.
Advances included Gunpowder weapons, the Magnetic Compass for navigation, and movable-type printing.
The examination system and Neo-Confucian thought shaped elite culture.
culture/song-dynasty.context: The Song built on the Han Dynasty tradition and was later conquered by the Mongol Empire.
culture/song-dynasty.observer: The Observer notes that a highly commercial, urbanized society experienced many innovations that later appeared elsewhere. The center of technological activity was not always where later histories place it.

culture/songhai-empire.title: Songhai Empire
culture/songhai-empire.summary: The Songhai Empire was a West African state that succeeded Mali as the dominant power on the Niger River from about 1464 until its defeat by a Moroccan army in 1591.
facts: Sunni Ali expanded the state and took Timbuktu in 1468.
Askia Muhammad organized a bureaucracy and promoted scholarship.
Trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt sustained it.
Moroccan forces with gunpowder firearms defeated it at Tondibi in 1591.
culture/songhai-empire.context: Songhai inherited the region of the Mali Empire and the scholarly city of Timbuktu. Its defeat shows the effect of Gunpowder weapons.
culture/songhai-empire.observer: The Observer notes that a large state was defeated by a smaller army with a newer weapon. Technology can overturn a balance of power quickly.
questions: How large was Songhai's army compared to the Moroccan force?

culture/srivijaya.title: Srivijaya
culture/srivijaya.summary: Srivijaya was a Buddhist maritime kingdom based at Palembang on Sumatra that dominated the Strait of Malacca and its trade from the 7th to the 13th century.
facts: The Chinese monk Yijing stayed in Srivijaya in 671 and reported on Buddhist study there.
The oldest known Srivijayan inscription, the Kedukan Bukit inscription, dates to 683.
It controlled shipping through the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait.
A naval expedition of the Chola king Rajendra I struck Srivijaya around 1025.
Its power faded in the 13th and 14th centuries, and it was absorbed by Java-based powers.
culture/srivijaya.context: Srivijaya was a hub of the Indian Ocean Trade Network, linking China and India. It was a Buddhist counterpart to the Hindu-Buddhist Angkor and Borobudur world, and clashed with the Chola Dynasty. Srivijaya sits in the Medieval Period and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Trade and Economy and Religion and Belief.
culture/srivijaya.observer: The Observer notes that the state's power rested on control of a strait and on the loyalty of port chiefs, not on a large territory. Power over movement can be more durable than power over land, until someone builds a faster route.
questions: How centralized was Srivijaya's rule?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Kedukan Bukit inscription (683 CE) is the oldest Srivijayan record; Rajendra Chola raided Srivijaya ports in 1025 [Wikipedia on the History of Srivijaya]

culture/sumerians.title: Sumerians
culture/sumerians.summary: The Sumerians were the people of southern Mesopotamia who built some of the world's first cities and developed cuneiform writing.
facts: Their city-states included Uruk, Ur, and Lagash.
They used cuneiform script on clay tablets for administration, literature, and law.
They built temple towers called ziggurats.
The Sumerian language is unrelated to any known living language family.
culture/sumerians.context: The Sumerians are central to Invention of Writing and The Urban Revolution. See Uruk and Mesopotamia.
culture/sumerians.observer: The Observer notes that a people who left no continuing language nonetheless left the technology of writing to the world. Cultural inheritance does not require survival of the culture.
questions: Where did the Sumerians come from?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Sumerian city-states included Eridu, Uruk, Ur and Lagash; cuneiform; Sumerian is a language isolate [World History Encyclopedia on Sumer]

culture/swahili-coast-city-states.title: Swahili Coast City-States
culture/swahili-coast-city-states.summary: The Swahili city-states were trading towns on the East African coast, including Kilwa, Mombasa, and Lamu, that flourished from about the 9th to the 15th century CE.
facts: They spoke Swahili, a Bantu language with many Arabic loanwords.
Coral-stone buildings and mosques characterized the towns.
Kilwa minted its own coins and exported gold from the interior; see Great Zimbabwe.
The traveler Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa in 1331; Portuguese attacks began in 1505.
culture/swahili-coast-city-states.context: These towns were nodes in the Indian Ocean Trade Network and grew from the Bantu Expansion. See Ibn Battuta.
culture/swahili-coast-city-states.observer: The Observer notes a culture created by mixing: African, Arab, and other traders and families forming a shared language and urban life.

culture/taino.title: Taino
culture/taino.summary: The Taino were an Arawakan-speaking people of the Greater Antilles and the Bahamas, who were the first Indigenous Americans encountered by Columbus in 1492.
facts: They lived in villages ruled by chiefs called caciques, and grew cassava, maize, and sweet potato.
They carved wooden and stone figures called zemis, associated with ancestors and spirits.
English words including canoe, hammock, hurricane, and barbecue come from Taino.
After 1492 their populations fell sharply because of disease, forced labor, and violence.
Genetic studies show Indigenous Caribbean ancestry survives in present-day Caribbean populations, contrary to the older idea that the Taino vanished.
culture/taino.context: The Taino were the first to experience the impact of the Columbian Exchange. The plantation economy that followed is described in Sugar Plantation Complex and the Atlantic Slave Trade. Taino sits in the Medieval Period and the region Caribbean and Atlantic World, and belongs to the theme thread of Kinship and Society and Religion and Belief.
culture/taino.observer: The Observer notes that several everyday words in English come from a language whose speakers were largely destroyed within a few decades. The words traveled as far as the people did not.
questions: What was the Taino population in 1492?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Greater Antilles chiefdoms led by caciques; zemis; canoe, hammock, hurricane and barbecue derive from Taino; 70-85 percent population loss; 61 percent of surveyed Puerto Ricans carry Indigenous mitochondrial DNA [Smithsonian Magazine on the Taino]

culture/tang-dynasty.title: Tang Dynasty
culture/tang-dynasty.summary: The Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907 CE and is regarded as a high point of Chinese poetry, art, and cosmopolitan culture.
facts: Its capital Chang'an was one of the world's largest cities, with about a million people.
Poets such as Li Bai and Du Fu wrote in this period.
The earliest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, was made in 868; see Woodblock Printing.
The An Lushan Rebellion (755 to 763) weakened the dynasty; death-toll estimates range from about 13 to 36 million and are disputed.
culture/tang-dynasty.context: The Tang followed the Han Dynasty tradition and preceded the Song Dynasty. Wu Zetian ruled during it.
culture/tang-dynasty.observer: The Observer notes a capital that hosted merchants, monks, and envoys from across Eurasia. A very connected city produces many new ideas, and also many new dependencies.
questions: What was the scale of the An Lushan Rebellion's toll?

culture/timurid-empire.title: Timurid Empire
culture/timurid-empire.summary: The Timurid Empire was a Turco-Mongol state founded by Timur in 1370 that ruled Central Asia and Iran, with Samarkand as its capital, and is remembered for its architecture and science.
facts: Timur took power in the region in 1370 and died in 1405.
After his death, his son Shah Rukh and grandson Ulugh Beg ruled key parts of the empire.
Ulugh Beg built a madrasa and an observatory at Samarkand in the 1410s and 1420s.
Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire, was a descendant of Timur.
culture/timurid-empire.context: The Timurids claimed the heritage of the Mongol Empire and passed their court culture to the Mughal Empire.
culture/timurid-empire.observer: The Observer notes a state that combined conquest with scholarship: the same dynasty produced massacres and a star catalogue. Power and learning can coexist in the same house.
questions: How united was the empire after Timur's death?

culture/tokugawa-shogunate.title: Tokugawa Shogunate
culture/tokugawa-shogunate.summary: The Tokugawa shogunate was the military government that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1867, a long period of peace and restricted foreign contact.
facts: Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun in 1603 and ruled from Edo (now Tokyo).
The policy known as 'sakoku' limited foreign trade, mainly to Dutch and Chinese merchants at Nagasaki.
Edo grew to about a million people, one of the world's largest cities.
The shogunate collapsed in 1867, and imperial rule was restored the following year in the Meiji Restoration.
culture/tokugawa-shogunate.context: The shogunate ruled through the Early Modern Period. See Meiji Restoration and Ming Dynasty for the neighboring Chinese state.
culture/tokugawa-shogunate.observer: The Observer notes a society that had a long internal peace and a developed urban culture with limited foreign contact. Peace let art and commerce flourish, and left the state unprepared for outside pressure.
questions: How isolated was Tokugawa Japan in practice?

culture/umayyad-caliphate.title: Umayyad Caliphate
culture/umayyad-caliphate.summary: The Umayyad Caliphate, ruling from Damascus from 661 to 750 CE, was the first hereditary dynasty of Islamic rulers and extended from Iberia to Sindh.
facts: Muawiya I founded the dynasty in 661 after the first civil war among Muslims.
Its armies conquered North Africa, most of Iberia (from 711), and Sindh (711).
Abd al-Malik completed the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem in 691 and reformed coinage and administration, making Arabic the language of government.
The Abbasid Revolution overthrew the dynasty in 750.
An Umayyad survivor, Abd al-Rahman I, founded a new Umayyad state in Cordoba in 756.
culture/umayyad-caliphate.context: The Umayyad Caliphate built the first large state of the Rise of Islam and was succeeded by the Abbasid Caliphate. Umayyad Caliphate sits in the Medieval Period and the region Levant and Anatolia, and belongs to the theme thread of Religion and Belief and War and Conflict and Language and Writing.
culture/umayyad-caliphate.observer: The Observer notes that within a century of Muhammad, a religious movement from the Arabian Peninsula had become an administrative empire that changed the language of government across three continents. Meaning-engines can also become bureaucracies.
questions: How quickly did conversion follow conquest?

culture/xiongnu.title: Xiongnu
culture/xiongnu.summary: The Xiongnu were a confederation of steppe peoples united under Modu Shanyu in 209 BCE, which became the first great steppe empire and the main rival of Han China.
facts: Chinese sources report that in 200 BCE Modu surrounded the Han emperor Gaozu at Baideng.
The Han then adopted the 'heqin' policy: marrying a princess to the ruler and sending annual gifts of silk, grain, and other goods.
The treaty was renewed many times until about 135 BCE.
The confederation split around 51 BCE, and the northern Xiongnu were defeated by Han and allied forces around 89 to 93 CE.
culture/xiongnu.context: The Xiongnu shaped the frontier policy of the Han Dynasty, following the Unification of China under Qin. They are the first in a line of steppe powers that culminated in the Mongol Empire.
culture/xiongnu.observer: The Observer notes how a mobile people without cities forced a large agrarian state to pay them for peace. Wealth flowed from the settled to the mobile, and that shaped both.
questions: How centralized was the Xiongnu confederation?

culture/yakut-sakha.title: Yakut (Sakha)
culture/yakut-sakha.summary: The Sakha (Yakut) are a Turkic-speaking people of northeastern Siberia who developed horse and cattle herding in one of the coldest inhabited regions on Earth; the timing of their northward migration is debated, but is often placed around the 13th to 15th centuries.
facts: Sakha is their own preferred name; the 2010 Russian census counted about 478,000 Sakha.
Russian penetration of the region began in the 17th century, and a major revolt against Russian rule occurred in 1642.
Yasak, a fur tribute, was levied on the Yakuts and neighboring peoples until 1917.
The Sakha supplied Russian expeditions with food, horses, and guides.
culture/yakut-sakha.context: The Sakha were incorporated in Russian Expansion into Siberia. See Siberia and the Arctic.
culture/yakut-sakha.observer: The Observer notes a herding culture built around horses in a land where winter temperatures fall far below what most of the species could endure. Cultural adaptation replaced biological adaptation.
questions: When and how did the Sakha's ancestors move north?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: 2010 census 478,085 Sakha; revolt 1642; yasak levied until 1917 [Minority Rights Group on the Sakha]

culture/yamnaya-culture.title: Yamnaya Culture
culture/yamnaya-culture.summary: The Yamnaya culture is an archaeological grouping of mobile pastoralists on the Pontic-Caspian steppe, in present Ukraine and southern Russia, usually dated about 3300 to 2600 BCE. Yamnaya-related ancestry spread across Eurasia, and the culture is central to debates over Indo-European origins.
facts: Yamnaya herders lived between the Dniester and Ural rivers, keeping cattle, sheep, goats and horses; few permanent settlements are known.
The name derives from Russian yama, "pit": the dead lay in pit graves under earthen mounds (kurgans), covered in red ochre.
Some graves held wagons or wagon parts, showing wheeled transport and suggesting modest social ranking, not cities or states.
From about 3100 BCE, Yamnaya-related groups moved west along the Danube into Hungary; Afanasievo burials in the Altai match Yamnaya ancestry closely.
Corded Ware groups, appearing in central Europe by about 2900 BCE, carried up to about 75 percent Yamnaya-like ancestry, though not all from known Yamnaya groups.
The Catacomb culture in the west and Poltavka on the middle Volga followed and overlapped Yamnaya.
culture/yamnaya-culture.context: Yamnaya belongs to the early Bronze Age of eastern Europe and preceded steppe societies such as the Sintashta Culture. Yamnaya wagons connect to The Wheel, Yamnaya ancestry to the Indo-European Language Spread. See Language and Writing, Technology and Kinship and Society.
culture/yamnaya-culture.observer: The Observer notes that Yamnaya herders raised kurgans across their seasonal grazing grounds, so the mounds may have served as claim-lines and grief-rites at once. Wagons in some graves read as status-signal built on a tool-lineage, and with no mark-code, mostly mounds and bones remain. A specialist could argue that the mounds' territorial role is inferred from placement rather than shown, which would weaken the claim-line reading.
questions: Did Yamnaya herders ride horses regularly, or mainly drive cattle-drawn wagons?
Did Yamnaya-related ancestry spread by migration, conquest, disease or gradual mixing, and did Yamnaya herders speak the ancestral Indo-European language?

culture/zagwe-dynasty.title: Zagwe Dynasty
culture/zagwe-dynasty.summary: The Zagwe dynasty ruled much of the Ethiopian highlands from about 1137 to 1270. Its best-known king, Lalibela, is remembered for a set of rock-hewn churches carved from living stone.
facts: The Zagwe dynasty ruled large parts of the Ethiopian highlands from about 1137 until 1270, when the last Zagwe king, Za-Ilmaknun, was killed in battle by the forces of the Amhara ruler Yekuno Amlak.

King Lalibela reigned about 1185 to 1225 and directed the carving of eleven monolithic churches from living rock at the Zagwe capital, which was later renamed for him. The churches are cut down into the rock below ground level and are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

In 1270 Yekuno Amlak founded a new dynasty, often called Solomonic, which ruled until 1974. Its rulers traced their descent to the biblical King Solomon through the royal house of Aksum, and dismissed the Zagwe as usurpers, describing their own rule as a restoration.
culture/zagwe-dynasty.context: The Zagwe followed the decline of the Kingdom of Aksum and preceded the long Solomonic line whose later rulers faced Italy at the Battle of Adwa.
culture/zagwe-dynasty.observer: The Observer notes that the dynasty that replaced the Zagwe wrote them down as usurpers and claimed an unbroken older lineage, so the account of the Zagwe survives largely through the story of their successors. The churches, by contrast, are a record the successors could not rewrite; see Who Writes the Record.
questions: How did the Zagwe understand their own legitimacy, given that the surviving account comes from their successors?
How were the Lalibela churches designed and built, and over how many years?

culture/zoroastrianism.title: Zoroastrianism
culture/zoroastrianism.summary: Zoroastrianism is an Iranian religion based on the teachings of Zarathustra, centered on the god Ahura Mazda and a moral struggle between truth and falsehood.
facts: Its oldest texts, the Gathas, are hymns attributed to Zarathustra in an archaic form of Iranian.
The date of Zarathustra is uncertain; scholars have proposed dates from about 1500 to about 600 BCE.
Its sacred collection is the Avesta.
The religion became the state religion of the Sasanian Empire (224 to 651 CE).
Zoroastrian communities persist in Iran and India, where they are called Parsis.
culture/zoroastrianism.context: Zoroastrianism shaped the religious world of the Achaemenid Persians, and is often discussed in connection with the Axial Age. After the Rise of Islam it became a minority faith. Zoroastrianism sits in the Iron Age and the region Iranian Plateau, and belongs to the theme thread of Religion and Belief.
culture/zoroastrianism.observer: The Observer notes that its emphasis on a cosmic struggle between order and disorder, and on a final judgment, resembles ideas found in later traditions, though the direction of influence is debated. The claim of borrowing would be weakened if independent origins were demonstrated.
questions: When did Zarathustra live?
How much did Zoroastrianism influence later religions?

culture/zulu-kingdom.title: Zulu Kingdom
culture/zulu-kingdom.summary: The Zulu Kingdom rose in southeastern Africa under Shaka from about 1816, and lasted until the British victory at Ulundi in 1879 ended its independence.
facts: Shaka turned the Zulu from one of many small Nguni clans into a large military state within a decade.
He introduced close-quarters fighting with short stabbing spears and regiment-based organization.
On 22 January 1879 a Zulu army destroyed a British column at Isandlwana, one of the greatest African victories over a European army.
The British won at Ulundi in July 1879, ending the independent kingdom.
culture/zulu-kingdom.context: See Shaka, Mfecane, and Scramble for Africa.
culture/zulu-kingdom.observer: The Observer notes that Zulu military organization was a social technology: regiments tied young men to the state in place of their families. Institutions can be more decisive than weapons.
questions: How much of Zulu power was due to Shaka's personal innovations?
